emotional_eating_frequency.graduation: Emotional eating 2-3 out of 10. Client identifies the emotion behind the urge in real time and chooses an alternative response most of the time. Occasional emotional eating is accepted without guilt.

portion_control.baseline: Regularly eats past full. Stops at stuffed, not satisfied. Ability to stop at satisfied: 3 out of 10.
portion_control.s3: Stops at satisfied 50 percent of the time. Notices the satisfied signal and responds to it. Ability: 5-6 out of 10.
portion_control.graduation: Stops at satisfied naturally at most meals. The satisfied signal is automatic and unmissable. Ability: 7-8 out of 10. Occasional overeating is human, not a crisis.

late_night_eating.baseline: Late-night eating 4-5 nights per week. After-9-PM eating driven by habit, loneliness, or stress.
late_night_eating.s3: Late-night eating reduced to 1-2 nights per week. Kitchen Closure anchor is active. Cravings recognized as waves and ridden out most nights.
late_night_eating.graduation: Late-night eating is rare (0-1 nights per week). The evening is filled with non-food activities. When a craving arises, it passes without action and without distress.

food_awareness.baseline: Low awareness of hungry versus eating-for-other-reasons. Awareness: 3 out of 10. Eating is often automatic and unconscious.
food_awareness.s3: Awareness increases to 6-7 out of 10. Client pauses before eating and asks 'am I hungry or feeding something else?' at most meals.
food_awareness.graduation: Awareness is 8-9 out of 10. Eating is a conscious act. The client knows why they are eating before they eat. Mindful eating is the default, not the exception.

weight_direction.baseline: Weight stable or increasing. BMI 32. Note: no specific weight-loss targets. The goal is behavioral change; weight follows behavior.
weight_direction.s3: Weight is trending in a healthier direction as a natural consequence of reduced emotional eating, improved portion awareness, and eliminated late-night eating. No scale targets set.
weight_direction.graduation: Weight has moved in a healthier direction as a natural byproduct of the behavioral changes. The client does not define success by the scale. Success is measured by the 6 SMART baselines, not pounds.

self_worth.baseline: Self-worth is tied to weight, eating behavior, and appearance. Guilt after eating is frequent. Confidence in ability to change: 4 out of 10.
self_worth.s3: Self-worth is decoupling from the scale. Guilt after eating is less frequent. Confidence: 6-7 out of 10. The client sees evidence that the pattern is changing.
self_worth.graduation: Self-worth is independent of weight. The client's identity has shifted from 'emotional eater' to 'conscious chooser.' Guilt after eating is rare and quickly resolved. Confidence: 8-9 out of 10.

session_script: [=== SESSION 1: INTAKE, ASSESSMENT, AND EMOTIONAL PAUSE INSTALLATION ===]
[--- WARM-UP AND RAPPORT (5 min) ---]

Jamie, welcome. Thank you for being here today. I know that taking this step takes courage, and I want you to know that this is a completely safe, judgment-free space. There is nothing you can say in this room that I have not heard before, and nothing you are dealing with that is unusual or shameful.

Before we begin, let me tell you what today looks like. We are going to have a conversation first. I am going to ask you some questions about your relationship with food, your eating patterns, and what is going on emotionally when the eating happens. Then I am going to explain how your mind works in a way that will make everything click. After that, we will do hypnosis. And you will leave today with a new tool installed in your subconscious that you can use immediately.
Sound good? Any questions before we start?
[--- L.O.V.E. INTAKE: LISTEN, OBSERVE, VERIFY, EMPATHIZE (15 min) ---]
[L: LISTEN -- open-ended, let them tell their story]
Tell me about your relationship with food. Not what you eat. How you eat. What role does food play in your life beyond keeping your body running?

[[Listen without interrupting. Note: emotional triggers, specific foods, timing patterns, body language when discussing shame/guilt. Watch for: downward gaze when discussing overeating (shame), hand-to-stomach gesture (somatic awareness), pace changes (speeds up when describing the cycle, slows when describing the wish for change).]]
[O: OBSERVE -- reflect what you see and hear]

I notice something important in what you just described. You said you know exactly what to eat, when to eat, how much to eat. The knowledge is all there. But something overrides that knowledge. Something automatic. Something that fires before you can think about it. Is that accurate?
[V: VERIFY -- confirm understanding, get specifics]
Let me make sure I have the full picture. Walk me through a typical day of eating. Start from the morning. What do you eat, when, and where?

[[Map the full daily timeline: breakfast, lunch, dinner, between-meal snacks, after-dinner eating. Identify: (1) which meals are normal versus excessive, (2) where the between-meal eating lives, (3) the critical evening window.]]
Good. Now tell me about the evening. After dinner. What happens between dinner and when you go to bed?
And when the late-night eating happens, what are you feeling right before you reach for the food? Not during. Not after. The moment before. What is the emotion?
[[Expected: stress, loneliness, boredom, dread, emptiness, restlessness. Get the specific emotion. This becomes the target for the Emotional Pause installation.]]
How many nights per week does this happen? Be specific.
And when you eat at night, what are you eating? What are the go-to comfort foods?
[E: EMPATHIZE -- validate, normalize, reframe]

Thank you for being honest about all of that. I want you to hear something clearly. What you just described is not a weakness. It is not a failure of discipline. It is not a character flaw. It is a pattern. An automatic program that your subconscious has been running for years because at some point in your life, it learned that food is the fastest way to change how you feel. And it was right. Food does change how you feel. Immediately. The problem is not that it works. The problem is what happens after.
[--- EATING PATTERN ASSESSMENT (5 min) ---]
Now I want to go deeper on the pattern itself. When you overeat, are you actually hungry? Physically hungry? Stomach empty, body needing fuel? Or is something else driving it?

That is the key distinction. Physical hunger builds gradually, can be satisfied by any food, and stops when the body has enough. Emotional hunger arrives suddenly, demands specific comfort foods, and does not stop when the body is full. Which one are you experiencing most of the time?
Have you tried diets before? Tell me which ones and what happened.

[[Expected: multiple diets, initial success, eventual regain. Listen for the breaking point: what specific event or emotion broke each diet? That breaking point reveals where the subconscious program is strongest.]]
What was the longest you sustained a change in eating? And what broke it? What was the specific moment the old pattern came back?
Here is a question that matters more than any number on a scale. If you could never change your weight, but you could change your relationship with food, what would that look like?
[[This answer reveals the real goal. Write it down verbatim. It becomes the treatment frame for the entire journey.]]
[--- SMART BASELINES (5 min) ---]

Before we go further, I want to establish six baselines. These are all on a 1-to-10 scale. Be honest. There are no right answers. I just need to know where you are today so we can measure the change over the coming sessions.
Number one. Control over eating decisions. 1 means you feel zero control, the eating happens to you. 10 means every bite is a fully conscious choice. Where are you today?

Number two. Awareness of hungry versus eating for other reasons. 1 means you have no idea which is driving you. 10 means you always know whether the drive is physical hunger or emotion. Where are you?
Number three. Ability to stop eating when satisfied. Not stuffed. Satisfied. The point where the body has had enough. 1 means you never stop there. 10 means you always stop at enough. Where are you?
Number four. Emotional eating frequency. How often is your eating driven by emotion rather than hunger? 1 means rarely. 10 means most meals are driven by emotion. Where are you?
Number five. Late-night or stress eating specifically. 1 means it never happens. 10 means it happens every night. Where are you?

Number six. Confidence in your ability to change these patterns. Not willpower. Confidence that the patterns can actually change. 1 means no confidence at all. 10 means absolute certainty. Where are you?
Good. I am recording all six. We will recheck them in two to three sessions and see where the numbers move.
[--- THEORY OF MIND FOR EATING (10 min, conscious education) ---]
Now let me explain what is actually happening in your mind when you overeat. Once you understand this, everything changes.

Your mind operates in two parts. The conscious mind handles about 12 percent of your mental processing. It is the part that knows what to eat, how much to eat, and when to stop. It is where your knowledge lives. It is where your willpower lives.
The subconscious mind handles the other 88 percent. It runs your heartbeat, your breathing, your digestion, your immune system. And it runs your automatic behaviors. Including your eating patterns.

At some point in your life, your subconscious learned a simple equation. Stress equals eat equals feel better. Loneliness equals eat equals comfort. Boredom equals eat equals stimulation. It learned this through thousands of repetitions. And now that equation runs automatically. Before the conscious mind can intervene, the hand is already reaching for the food.

That is why willpower fails. Every time. You are deploying 12 percent of your mental resources against 88 percent. The math does not work. It never will. That is not a character flaw. That is architecture.

Here is the chemistry behind it. Eating triggers dopamine, the reward chemical. Your brain says: that felt good, do it again. Food, especially sugar, fat, and salt, triggers a significant dopamine release. Your gut also produces roughly 90 to 95 percent of the body's serotonin, the calm-and-content chemical. So when you eat, you are literally changing your brain chemistry. The comfort is real. The relief is real. It is neurochemical, not imaginary.

But the effect is temporary. Minutes. Then the dopamine drops. The guilt arrives. The frustration. The self-criticism. And those emotions are themselves triggers for more eating. Trigger, eat, guilt, trigger, eat. The cycle reinforces itself every single time it runs.
We do not fight this cycle with willpower. We update the program. We install a new instruction in the 88 percent so the automatic response changes at the source.
[--- THE EMOTIONAL PAUSE CONCEPT (conscious, pre-trance) ---]
Right now, the pattern runs like this: trigger, then eat. No gap. No pause. No choice. The trigger fires and the hand reaches for food before the conscious mind even registers what happened.
What we install today is a pause between the trigger and the action. The new pattern becomes: trigger, pause, choose, act.

In that pause, which lasts about five seconds, one question rises from your subconscious. Not from willpower. From the deeper mind. The question is: What do I actually need right now? Am I hungry? Or am I feeding something else?
If the answer is hungry, the pause releases. You eat. You enjoy it. No guilt. No shame. Food is fuel and the body deserves fuel.

If the answer is something else, the pause holds. And in that held space, you choose. Breathe. Move. Call someone. Step outside. Drink water. The craving is a wave. It peaks in about 90 seconds and then it passes. Every time. If you can ride 90 seconds, the wave passes. And each time you ride it, the next wave is smaller.

That is what we install today. The Emotional Pause. It goes into the 88 percent. It runs automatically. It does not require willpower. It fires on its own, every time a trigger activates, for the rest of your life.
[--- SUGGESTIBILITY TEST SETUP ---]

Before we begin the hypnosis, I want to do a brief exercise that helps me understand how your mind processes information. This is not a test you pass or fail. It simply shows me whether your subconscious responds more to direct instruction or to indirect imagery. That information helps me tailor everything we do today to the way your mind works best.

[[Run standard suggestibility test: arm rigidity, eye closure, hand clasp, or lemon test depending on client comfort. For Jamie (62% Emotional, Visual), the lemon visualization or book-and-balloon typically work well. Score and note EP confirmation or shift.]]
[--- INDUCTION: ARM-RAISING ---]
[EMOTIONAL LANE (62% Emotional -- primary approach)]
I would like you to sit comfortably with both feet flat on the floor. Place your hands on your thighs, palms down. If you are wearing glasses, please remove them.
Now raise your right arm and bend it at the elbow, placing the palm of your hand in front of your face, about ten inches away, with your fingers pointing upward and above eye level.

Good. Stare at your middle finger. Take a deep, comfortable breath. And on the exhale, you may notice that your fingers begin to separate. Gently. Naturally. Wider and wider, further and further apart.
Now I am going to ask you a few questions. Rather than answering out loud, just nod your head yes or no.

Have you ever been so absorbed in a movie or a book that you forgot where you were? Have you ever driven somewhere and arrived without remembering the drive? Have you ever been so deep in thought that someone had to say your name twice before you heard them?
Good. Can you visualize your hand as it rests in front of you right now? Can you see every detail? The texture of the skin. The lines on your palm. The shape of each finger? Hold that image.
Now I want you to notice something. I will notice the changes happening in your body before you do. When you notice them yourself, simply nod yes.
Your breathing is beginning to deepen. You are taking in more oxygen. When you notice your breathing getting deeper, nod yes.
Your eyelids may begin to flutter. This rapid movement is a natural sign that you are entering the first stages of hypnosis. When you notice this fluttering, nod yes.
Notice that one hand feels heavier against your leg, while the other, the one in front of your face, feels lighter. As if something gentle is lifting it. When you feel this difference, nod yes.

That lightness is growing. Your hand is becoming lighter and lighter. Rising gently. Lifting. Turning slowly inward. Moving closer to your face. Whether your head comes down to meet your hand or your hand rises to meet your face, allow it to happen at whatever pace feels right.
The moment your hand touches your forehead, give me a nod. At that instant you will reach your peak of suggestibility and enter the hypnotic state.
[Wait for contact and nod.] Deep Sleep.

Each and every time I suggest the words Deep Sleep to you, for the purpose of hypnosis and with your permission, you will enter this state of hypnosis very quickly, calmly, and deeply, and the physical body will relax.
[PHYSICAL LANE BRANCH (use if EP tested Physical)]

[[If suggestibility testing reveals a physical dominant: switch to direct language. 'Stare at your middle finger. Your fingers ARE separating. Your hand IS rising. You WILL feel the difference.' Power words: NOW, IMMEDIATELY, AUTOMATICALLY. Same induction structure, different tone and verb force.]]
[--- DEEPENING: 5-0 COUNT + PHS ---]
Now you can gently allow your hand to float back down to rest comfortably on your lap.
As I count from five down to zero, each number will take you deeper into this comfortable, heavy relaxation.
Five. Going down now. Deeper and deeper. Your body beginning to let go.
Four. Physically releasing. Every muscle softening.
Three. Emotionally calm. Peaceful. Safe.
Two. Mentally quiet. The noise of the day fading.
One. Deeper still. Drifting down.
Zero. [Snap.] Deep Sleep.

Each and every time I suggest the words Deep Sleep to you, for the purpose of hypnosis and with your permission, you will enter this state of hypnosis very quickly, calmly, and deeply, and the physical body will relax.
[--- PROGRESSIVE RELAXATION: BODY RECONNECTION ---]

Now as you rest in this comfortable state, I want you to reconnect with your body. Because your body has been trying to talk to you. It sends signals all day long. Full. Hungry. Tired. Satisfied. And those signals have been drowned out by the noise, the stress, the emotions. Today we turn the volume back up.

Starting at the top of your head. A warm wave of relaxation begins to flow downward. Your scalp softens. Your forehead smooths. The muscles around your eyes release. Your jaw unclenches. And as it does, notice how your body feels when it lets go. That feeling of release. That is your body talking. It is saying: thank you.

The wave moves through your neck. Your shoulders drop. The tension that has been sitting there, maybe for days, maybe for years, it dissolves. Down through your arms. Your hands. Your fingers. Warm. Heavy. Still.

Your chest opens. Your breathing deepens. And now bring your awareness to your stomach. Place your attention there gently. Your stomach is one of the most intelligent organs in your body. It knows exactly when it has had enough. It has been sending that signal your entire life. We are turning up the volume on that signal today.
The warm wave continues. Down through your hips. Your legs. Your feet. Every part of you sinking deeper. Heavier. More connected to the body that has been waiting for you to listen.
Five. Four. Three. Two. One. Zero. [Snap.] Deep Sleep.
[Repeat PHS.]
[--- EMOTIONAL PAUSE INSTALLATION (first taste -- in trance) ---]
Now I want you to imagine a scene. You are at home. It is evening. Around nine o'clock. You have already eaten dinner. The dinner was enough. Your body is satisfied.

And now the feeling arrives. That familiar pull. The restlessness. The urge. Maybe it is stress from the day. Maybe it is the quiet of the apartment. Maybe it is just habit. The old program is firing. It is pointing you toward the kitchen.

But this time, something is different. Between the urge and the action, there is a space. A pause. Like a doorway that was not there before. And in that doorway, a single question forms. Not from willpower. From somewhere deeper. From the part of you that knows the truth.
What do I actually need right now?
Am I hungry? Or am I feeding something else?

And you listen. You listen to your stomach. It is calm. It is satisfied. It does not need food. The hunger is not in your stomach. It is in your chest. It is loneliness. Or stress. Or habit. And now you know.

The pause holds. The doorway stays open. And you choose. You choose to breathe. Three slow breaths. You choose to feel the feeling without feeding it. You choose to let the wave rise and peak and pass. And it does pass. In about 90 seconds. It always passes.

And when it passes, notice what is left. Calm. Clarity. A quiet pride. You did not fight the urge. You did not white-knuckle through it. You simply paused. You asked the question. And you chose. That is the new program. Trigger. Pause. Choose. Act.

This pause is installing itself in your subconscious right now. Deeply. Permanently. From this moment forward, every time an emotional trigger fires, the pause activates automatically. You do not have to remember it. You do not have to force it. It is part of your operating system now. It fires on its own.
And these suggestions grow stronger day by day. Stronger by the hour. Stronger by the minute. They are firmly embedded in your subconscious mind. And they belong to you. They are yours.
[--- COUNT OUT + HOMEWORK ---]
Now I am going to count from zero up to five. With each number you will become more alert, more awake, more refreshed, with a wonderful feeling of confidence and calm.

Zero. I am closing the door to the subconscious mind, sealing in every suggestion. The Emotional Pause is installed. The body connection is restored. The new program is running. Sealing in everything we built today. Sealing out the old automatic cycle.
One. Slowly and calmly beginning to come up.
Two. Becoming more physically aware, more mentally alert. Knowing that tonight, the next time you feel the pull toward the kitchen, the pause will be there. Automatic. Effortless.
Three. Coming up higher now. Feeling wonderful. Feeling lighter. Not because the weight changed. Because the relationship with food just changed.
Four. Your eyes are beginning to open.
Five. Eyes open, wide awake. Fully alert, refreshed, and confident. Welcome back.
One, two, three, four, five. Eyes open, wide awake.
[--- POST-SESSION: HOMEWORK ASSIGNMENT ---]
Before you go, here is what I need from you between now and Session 2. Three things.

First. Keep a food journal. Not calories. Not macros. Write down three things every time you eat: what you ate, what time it was, and what emotion you were feeling. That emotion column is the important one. You will start seeing the pattern on paper.

Second. Practice the Emotional Pause three times a day. Not just when cravings hit. Practice it at mealtimes too. Before each meal, take one breath and ask: am I hungry, or am I feeding something else? If hungry, eat and enjoy. If something else, notice it and choose.

Third. This week, when the late-night urge arrives, try one thing differently. Instead of going to the kitchen, sit with the feeling for 90 seconds. Just 90 seconds. Set a timer if you need to. Notice the wave rise. Notice it peak. And notice it pass. You do not have to do this every night. Just once. One successful ride proves the wave passes.
That is the homework. Food journal with emotions. Pause practice three times a day. One craving ride.
[[Schedule Session 2 within 1-2 weeks. Momentum matters. If the client cannot do next week, two weeks maximum.]]

One more thing. If between now and our next session you have a night where the old pattern runs, where you eat when you did not want to, do not beat yourself up about it. That is the old program firing. It does not erase what we built today. The pause is installed. It may not catch every trigger immediately. But it is there. And it gets stronger every day. What matters is not perfection. What matters is that the pause showed up at least once. That one pause is proof the program is running.
I will see you at Session 2.
[=== POST-SESSION THERAPIST CHECKLIST ===]

[[1. Record all 6 SMART baselines. 2. Note specific triggers identified (which emotions, which times, which foods). 3. Note EP confirmation or shift. 4. Note client's verbatim answer to 'what would your relationship with food look like?' 5. Note any contraindication flags (ED symptoms, depression indicators, medication use). 6. Plan Session 2 focus based on intake findings: if late-night eating is dominant, prioritize Kitchen Closure. If emotional triggers are diffuse, prioritize Satisfied Signal and general mindfulness. If root cause material surfaced strongly, consider moving Root Cause Processing earlier. 7. Send AVS within 24 hours.]]

cases.title: Binge Eating: The Loss of Control Spiral
cases.presenting: I eat normally all day. Breakfast, lunch, even dinner is fine. But then something happens at night. It is like a switch flips in my brain and I just... consume. Pizza, burgers, whatever I can order. Three thousand, four thousand calories in one sitting. I cannot stop once it starts. Afterward I feel disgusted with myself. I swear I will never do it again. And then two days later, the switch flips again. I have gained sixty pounds in three years and nobody at work even knows this is happening.

client.name: Marcus T.
client.history: Binge eating episodes 3-4 times per week. Eats normally during the day, then consumes 3000-4000 calories in one sitting at night. Feels complete loss of control — describes it as a switch flips. Followed by intense shame and guilt. Has gained 60 pounds over 3 years. No purging behaviors. Not formally diagnosed with BED but pattern matches. Previous attempt with CBT helped understand the cycle but did not stop it. Divorced, lives alone, binge episodes worse on weekends. Comfort foods: pizza, fast food, anything he can order and eat fast. Hides the behavior — nobody at work knows.

intake_dialogue.text: Marcus, I want to understand what happens during a binge episode. Not the food itself, but the experience. Walk me through one from beginning to end. What does it feel like when it starts?

It starts with a feeling. Not hunger. I am not hungry. It is like a pressure that builds during the day and by evening it is unbearable. I will be sitting at my desk coding and I know, I just know, tonight is going to be a binge night. There is a moment where something flips. Before the flip I am fine. After the flip I am already ordering food on my phone. It happens that fast.

That switch you are describing is not weakness, Marcus. That is your subconscious activating a program. It has learned a sequence: pressure builds, threshold is reached, emergency protocol fires. The binge is the emergency protocol. Your deeper mind genuinely believes it is helping you survive something.

Survive what though? My life is fine. I have a good job. I am not starving. There is no emergency. But my body acts like there is. And then afterward, the shame. I sit there surrounded by empty containers and I hate myself. I literally cannot look at myself. I clean everything up immediately so there is no evidence. I take the trash out to the dumpster at midnight so my neighbors do not see the bags.

That shame is not just a consequence of the binge. It is fuel for the next one. The cycle works like this: pressure builds, the switch flips, you binge, the shame hits, the shame becomes pressure, and the pressure builds again. The shame is not separate from the problem. It is part of the engine that drives it.

I never thought of it that way. I always thought if I could just feel bad enough about it, I would stop. So I punish myself. I skip meals the next day. I go to the gym and destroy myself. I promise I will never do it again. And then Friday night comes around and I am alone and the switch flips and it all starts over.
Tell me about the timing. You mentioned weekends are worse. What is different about weekends? And is there a pattern with being alone?

Weekends are the worst because there is no structure. At work I have meetings, deadlines, people around me. I do not binge at work. I do not even think about it. But Friday evening I walk into my empty apartment and there is nothing between me and the food. Saturday is wide open. Sunday too. Since the divorce it has gotten so much worse. When Sarah was here there was accountability. Someone would see. Now there is nobody to see.

Let me ask you something that might surprise you. If you could never change your weight but you could completely change your relationship with food, if you could eat without the switch ever flipping, without the shame, without the hiding, what would that look like for you?

I just want to eat like a normal person. I want to order a pizza and eat two slices and put the rest in the fridge. I want to go to a restaurant and not eat everything on the plate plus the bread basket. I want to stop thinking about food as the enemy and the only friend at the same time. I just want to be normal with food.

clinical_notes.theory_of_mind: Binge eating in this client represents environmental hypnosis — the subconscious has learned that when stress and loneliness overload the message units, the fastest escape route is through massive food consumption. The 88 percent runs a deeply reinforced emergency protocol: overwhelm threshold reached, initiate binge, flood the system with dopamine, achieve temporary numbness, crash into shame, use shame as evidence of brokenness, which generates more overwhelm, which lowers the threshold for the next binge. The switch Marcus describes is the moment the subconscious overrides the conscious mind entirely. The 12 percent goes offline. The binge is not a choice — it is a dissociative escape response mediated through food. The hiding behavior indicates the subconscious knows the behavior is problematic but categorizes exposure as a greater threat than the binge itself. Structure (work, people, routine) provides enough external regulation to prevent threshold breach during the day. Without structure (evenings, weekends, post-divorce solitude), the internal pressure has no outlet except the learned one.
clinical_notes.ep_approach: 54% Physical — slightly Physical-dominant, essentially balanced. Use a hybrid delivery approach. For behavioral interruption techniques (the speed bump, the binge interrupt), use direct Physical-lane language: clear, specific, authoritative. Your hand stops. You put the phone down. The order does not get placed. For emotional processing (shame dissolution, divorce grief, loneliness), shift to Emotional-lane delivery: permissive, metaphorical, indirect. You may notice the shame beginning to dissolve. Allow yourself to feel what is underneath. The balanced EP means Marcus can receive both modalities. Lead with Physical for behavioral change, shift to Emotional for depth work.
clinical_notes.key_reframe: Bingeing is your brain's emergency exit. At some point your subconscious learned that when the pressure becomes unbearable, food is the fastest way to flood the system with enough dopamine to create temporary numbness. It is an escape hatch, not a moral failure. The switch that flips is your subconscious saying: emergency protocol activated. We are not going to shame you out of the emergency exit. That has never worked and it never will, because shame IS the pressure that triggers the next emergency. Instead, we are going to build a better exit. One that actually resolves the pressure instead of just numbing it temporarily.
clinical_notes.contraindications: SCREEN for Binge Eating Disorder (BED). If the client meets DSM-5 criteria (recurrent episodes, marked distress, at least once per week for 3 months, absence of compensatory behaviors), refer to a licensed therapist or psychiatrist for formal diagnosis. Hypnotherapy can complement BED treatment but should not be the sole intervention for a clinical eating disorder. Screen for depression — binge eating is frequently comorbid with major depressive disorder, and the shame-isolation cycle raises concern. Screen for alcohol or substance use — cross-addiction is common in binge patterns, and the loss-of-control description could indicate broader impulse regulation challenges. Screen for suicidal ideation — the shame cycle, social isolation, hiding behavior, and self-described self-hatred warrant careful assessment. If purging behaviors are present (vomiting, laxative use, excessive compensatory exercise beyond normal fitness), REFER immediately — bulimia nervosa requires specialized treatment.
clinical_notes.root_cause_assessment: Loneliness and loss of structure post-divorce. Sarah provided external regulation (accountability, witness, shared meals, emotional connection). Her absence removed the scaffolding that kept the binge pattern contained. Weekend isolation eliminates all external structure. The empty apartment is the trigger environment. Childhood exploration needed: was food used as reward or punishment? Was eating fast normalized (food scarcity, mealtime conflict)? Was emotional expression allowed, or was it suppressed (leading to food as the only permitted outlet)? The hiding behavior suggests deep shame conditioning — where did Marcus learn that being seen in a vulnerable state is dangerous? The speed of consumption suggests the binge serves a dissociative function — the goal is not taste or pleasure but rapid neurochemical state change.
clinical_notes.neurochemistry: Binge eating creates a massive dopamine spike far larger than normal eating — the sheer volume and speed of consumption floods the reward system. The brain becomes habituated to this supranormal spike, and normal meals feel neurochemically flat by comparison. This is tolerance, the same mechanism that drives substance dependency. The post-binge crash triggers a cortisol surge (shame, self-hatred, anxiety) which the subconscious recognizes as a threat state. The fastest known remedy for the cortisol threat state is another dopamine flood, which primes the next binge. Additionally, the restriction pattern (skipping meals after a binge) creates genuine caloric deficit, triggering ghrelin elevation and leptin suppression, which lowers the threshold for the next binge. Breaking the cycle requires: (1) interrupt the trigger-to-binge link before the switch flips, (2) provide alternative dopamine sources, (3) dissolve the shame that generates the cortisol that fuels the cycle, (4) eliminate the restriction pattern that creates biological vulnerability.
clinical_notes.evidence_base: Stradling 1998 (Oxford): hypnotherapy combined with stress reduction maintained 3.8 kg weight loss at 18-month follow-up. HYPNODIET randomized controlled trial: 67.7 percent of hypnotherapy group normalized eating disinhibition scores. Kirsch 1995 meta-analysis: CBT plus hypnosis significantly outperformed CBT alone for weight management, with benefits tripling after treatment ended. Emotion-Focused Therapy pilot studies showed significant reduction in binge episodes when emotional processing was paired with behavioral interruption. BED prevalence is estimated at 20 to 30 percent in treatment-seeking obese populations. Telch 2001: group CBT for BED reduced binge episodes by 48 percent at end of treatment and 64 percent at 6-month follow-up.

session_plan.pretalk_focus: Theory of Mind applied to binge eating. The 88/12 split: why the switch flips and why willpower cannot prevent it. The neurochemistry of the binge-shame-binge cycle (dopamine flood, cortisol crash, repeat). The restrict-binge trap: why punishing yourself with restriction makes the next binge MORE likely, not less. The concept of the Speed Bump: installing a 10-second interruption before the switch flips. The switch does not flip instantly — there is a 5-to-10-second window where intervention is possible.
session_plan.induction: Arm-raising (standard). Hybrid approach for 54% Physical. Lead with direct language for initial compliance — Your fingers are separating, your hand IS rising — then shift to permissive layering once in trance. For Physical-dominant moments: Now, immediately, your body responds. For Emotional undercurrent: You may notice, allowing, drifting. The balanced EP means the induction can flex between modalities based on real-time responsiveness.
deepeners: 5-0 Count with PHS (standard foundation)
Reactional x2-4 (deepen and verify depth)
Progressive Relaxation with emphasis on stomach awareness and the body's natural fullness signals
Control Room Deepener: descend into a control room where the binge switch is visible as a physical lever — a speed bump can be installed in front of it
therapy: Binge Interrupt Installation (The Speed Bump): the core Session 1 intervention. Before the switch flips, there is a 5-to-10-second window. In that window, the phone is still in the hand but the order has not been placed. Install a speed bump: a physical sensation (heaviness in the hands, warmth in the stomach) paired with one question from the subconscious — Do I want to feel this way in 30 minutes? The speed bump fires automatically every time the switch begins to engage.

Shame Dissolution: shame is not truth and shame is not identity. The shame that follows a binge is a feeling, not a fact. Install the reframe: when shame arrives after eating, it is recognized as the old cycle trying to reload. Instead of shame fueling the next binge, shame is met with one thought — that was the old program, it does not define me, and it has less power every time it runs.

Alternative Dopamine Sources: the subconscious needs dopamine — that is non-negotiable. Install three alternative pathways: movement (even 10 minutes of walking changes neurochemistry), connection (calling someone, texting, being in the presence of another human), creation (coding a personal project, building something, any generative activity). These provide the subconscious with options so the emergency exit is not the only available door.

Portion Pacing Protocol: binge eating is characterized by speed. Install a pacing intervention: slow down, taste the first three bites fully, put the fork down between bites, one breath between bites. Speed is the vehicle of the binge. Remove the speed and the binge mechanism stalls.

Weekend Structure Plan: isolation and lack of structure are the primary triggers. Install weekend anchors — three pre-planned activities for morning, afternoon, and evening that create structure in unstructured time. The goal is to prevent the empty-apartment-nothing-to-do state that lowers the binge threshold.

Future Self Visualization: Normal Eater. Meet the version of Marcus six months from now who orders a pizza and eats two slices and puts the rest away. Who spends Friday evening alone and the switch does not flip. That version is not thin. He is free. And he is already being built starting today.
session_plan.countout: Standard 0-5 with suggestion seal. Zero seals in the Speed Bump, the Shame Dissolution reframe, the Alternative Dopamine pathways, and the Portion Pacing protocol. All locked into the subconscious, growing stronger every day, every meal, every time the old switch tries to engage and finds a speed bump in the way. Five brings full alertness with calm confidence.

sessions.title: Intake, Assessment, and Binge Interrupt Installation
sessions.focus: L.O.V.E. intake for binge eating patterns. Map the switch: what happens before, during, and after a binge episode. Identify environmental triggers (weekends, isolation, empty apartment, lack of structure). Establish 6 SMART baselines (1-10 subjective scales). Theory of Mind for binge eating. Suggestibility testing (confirm Physical-dominant hybrid). First induction. Install Speed Bump (the 10-second interrupt before the switch flips). Homework: binge journal (date, time, trigger, what happened in the 10 seconds before, food consumed, duration, feeling after), practice recognizing the pre-switch window 3x daily.

sessions.title: Shame Dissolution and the Restrict-Binge Trap
sessions.focus: Review binge journal patterns. Address the shame cycle directly: shame is fuel, not medicine. Dismantle the restriction pattern (skipping meals after a binge increases biological vulnerability). Install consistent eating structure: three meals daily regardless of what happened the night before. Shame dissolution in trance. Homework: eat three meals every day this week regardless of binge episodes. No punishment. No restriction.

sessions.title: Alternative Dopamine and the Emergency Exit Upgrade
sessions.focus: Deepen trance. Install three alternative dopamine pathways (movement, connection, creation). The emergency exit still exists but now there are three additional doors. In trance: visualize pressure building, threshold approaching, and three new doors appearing. Practice choosing a new door. Reinforce Speed Bump. Homework: when pre-binge feeling arrives, try one alternative before the binge. If binge still happens, acceptable — the goal is inserting one attempt.

sessions.title: Portion Pacing and Speed Disruption
sessions.focus: Address the speed component of bingeing. Introduce Portion Pacing: first three bites tasted fully, fork down between bites, one breath between bites. Practice in trance with a visualized meal. Install: fast eating serves the binge program, slow eating serves you. Reinforce all prior installations. Homework: practice pacing at one meal per day, aim for 20 minutes per meal.

sessions.title: Root Cause Processing: Divorce, Isolation, and the Empty Apartment
sessions.focus: Deeper trance. Process divorce grief and loss of external regulation. Explore what the empty apartment represents. Process the core emotion in trance. Thank the binge pattern for protecting Marcus during the worst of the divorce. Release it with gratitude. Homework: write a letter to the binge pattern — what it gave you, what it cost you, what you choose now.

sessions.title: Weekend Structure and Environmental Redesign
sessions.focus: Address the weekend trigger environment directly. Install weekend anchors (morning, afternoon, evening activities). Restructure relationship with the apartment. In trance: visualize a structured weekend from start to finish. Solitude is not loneliness. Marcus can be alone without being lonely. Reinforce all installations. Homework: implement weekend anchors, log how binge urge responds to structure.

sessions.title: Future Self Integration and Identity Rebuild
sessions.focus: Future Self visualization: the normal eater. Identity-level integration: I am a person who eats when hungry and stops when satisfied. I am not broken. I was running an outdated program and I have updated it. Review SMART baselines. Homework: daily self-hypnosis, continue binge journal.

sessions.title: Graduation, Self-Hypnosis Mastery, and Relapse Prevention
sessions.focus: Final SMART baseline review. Install relapse prevention: one binge episode does not reset progress. The speed bump is permanent. Teach formal self-hypnosis. Install anchor: both hands flat on thighs, three breaths, speed bump reactivates. Discuss booster sessions. Graduation: your subconscious updated its emergency protocol. The old exit is still there. It is just not the only exit anymore.

binge_frequency.baseline: Binge episodes 3-4 times per week. Complete loss of control during episodes. Frequency: 8-9 out of 10.
binge_frequency.s3: Binge episodes reduced to 1-2 per week. Speed Bump engaging before most episodes. Some episodes interrupted before full binge. Frequency: 5-6 out of 10.
binge_frequency.graduation: Binge episodes rare (0-1 per month). The switch still tries to flip occasionally but the Speed Bump catches it. When an episode occurs, it is shorter, smaller, and followed by self-compassion instead of shame. Frequency: 2-3 out of 10.

control_during_episodes.baseline: Zero sense of control once the switch flips. The binge runs to completion every time. Control: 1-2 out of 10.
control_during_episodes.s3: Some episodes can be interrupted mid-binge. The Speed Bump creates a window of awareness even during an episode. Portion Pacing slows consumption. Control: 4-5 out of 10.
control_during_episodes.graduation: Even when the urge arises, Marcus can choose to eat a portion instead of bingeing. The all-or-nothing pattern is broken. Control: 7-8 out of 10.

shame_level.baseline: Intense shame and self-hatred after every episode. Shame drives hiding, restriction, and the next binge. Shame severity: 9-10 out of 10.
shame_level.s3: Shame still present but recognized as a feeling, not a fact. The shame-to-restriction pipeline is disrupted. Marcus eats normally the day after an episode. Shame: 5-6 out of 10.
shame_level.graduation: Shame is rare and brief. Met with self-compassion. The shame-binge cycle is broken. Shame: 2-3 out of 10.

hiding_behavior.baseline: Complete secrecy. Nobody knows about the bingeing. Evidence destroyed immediately. Midnight trash runs. Hiding: 9-10 out of 10.
hiding_behavior.s3: Has told at least one person about the pattern. Hiding behavior reduced. Beginning to accept this is a challenge, not a secret. Hiding: 5-6 out of 10.
hiding_behavior.graduation: No longer defines the pattern as a shameful secret. Can discuss eating challenges openly with trusted people. Hiding: 2-3 out of 10.

weekend_structure.baseline: Weekends are unstructured and isolated. No plans, no social contact, no anchors. Structure: 2 out of 10.
weekend_structure.s3: Weekend anchors in place for at least 2 of 3 time blocks. At least one social interaction per weekend. Structure: 5-6 out of 10.
weekend_structure.graduation: Weekends have reliable structure without rigidity. Regular activities and social connections. Solitude is chosen, not suffered. Structure: 7-8 out of 10.

self_worth.baseline: Self-worth deeply eroded by the binge pattern. Marcus describes self-hatred, disgust, and brokenness. Worth: 2-3 out of 10.
self_worth.s3: Self-worth decoupling from eating behavior. Worth beginning to be sourced from other areas of life. Worth: 5-6 out of 10.
self_worth.graduation: Self-worth independent of eating behavior. Identity shifted from someone who binges in secret to someone who faced a difficult pattern and changed it. Worth: 7-8 out of 10.

session_script: [=== SESSION 1: INTAKE, ASSESSMENT, AND BINGE INTERRUPT INSTALLATION ===]
[--- WARM-UP AND RAPPORT (5 min) ---]

Marcus, welcome. Thank you for coming in today. I want you to know something right from the start. Whatever you tell me in this room stays in this room, and nothing you describe will surprise or shock me. You mentioned on the phone that you have been dealing with a pattern around food that feels out of control. That takes courage to acknowledge. Let us talk about it openly.

Here is how today works. First, we have a conversation. I am going to ask you about the eating pattern, what triggers it, what happens during and after. Then I will explain exactly what is happening in your brain when the pattern fires and why willpower has not been able to stop it. After that, we do hypnosis. And you leave today with a tool installed in your subconscious that you can use immediately. Sound good?
[--- L.O.V.E. INTAKE: LISTEN, OBSERVE, VERIFY, EMPATHIZE (15 min) ---]
[L: LISTEN -- open-ended exploration]
Tell me about what happens when you binge. Not what you eat. What the experience is like. From the first moment you know it is coming to the moment it is over.

[[Listen fully. Note: the switch metaphor, speed of consumption, hiding behavior, emotional sequence (pressure, flip, consume, crash, shame). Watch body language: does he break eye contact when describing the behavior? Hands covering stomach? Voice drops? These indicate shame activation in real time.]]
[O: OBSERVE -- reflect the pattern]

I hear two things in what you described. First, the switch. There is a moment of transition from in-control to out-of-control and it feels instantaneous. Second, the hiding. You go to significant effort to make sure nobody sees this part of your life. Both tell me something important about how your subconscious is processing this pattern.
[V: VERIFY -- get the specifics]
How many times per week does this happen? Be as accurate as you can.
And what time of day? Is it always evening, or does it happen at other times?
Tell me about the foods. What are you reaching for? And how fast are you eating?

[[Map the binge profile: frequency (3-4x/week), timing (evenings, worse weekends), foods (delivery, fast food, high-calorie, speed-optimized), duration, volume (3000-4000 calories), and aftermath (shame, hiding, restriction next day).]]
What happens the day after a binge? How do you handle it?
[[Listen for restriction: skipping meals, over-exercising, self-punishment. The restrict-binge cycle is biochemically reinforced and must be addressed.]]
How long has this pattern been going on? And has anything changed recently that made it worse?
[E: EMPATHIZE -- validate and reframe]

Marcus, I want to say this directly because I think you need to hear it from someone. What you just described is not a character flaw. It is not weakness. It is a pattern that your subconscious installed because at some point it learned that massive food consumption is the fastest way to change your neurochemical state when the pressure becomes unbearable. And honestly, it works. The problem is not that it does not work. The problem is the cost.
[--- BINGE PATTERN ANALYSIS (5 min) ---]

I want to understand the switch more precisely. You said it flips and then you are already ordering food. But I want to slow that moment down. Before the switch flips, is there a feeling? A physical sensation? Something in your body that tells you it is coming?
[[Critical: the speed bump must be installed in the pre-switch window. If client identifies a somatic precursor (chest tightness, restlessness, jaw clenching), that becomes the trigger.]]

That feeling you just described is the 10-second window. Between that feeling and the switch flipping, there are about 5 to 10 seconds. Right now those seconds pass unnoticed. What we do today is install a speed bump in those 10 seconds.

Now let me ask the big question. If you could never change your weight, not one pound, but you could change your relationship with food so the switch never flips again, no bingeing, no hiding, no shame, what would that look like?
[[Record verbatim. This is the treatment frame.]]
[--- SMART BASELINES (5 min) ---]
Before we continue, I need six baseline numbers from you. All on a 1-to-10 scale. Be honest. These are not grades. They are coordinates.
Number one. Binge frequency. 1 means it rarely happens. 10 means almost every day. Where are you?
Number two. Sense of control during an episode. 1 means zero control. 10 means you can always stop when you choose to. Where are you?
Number three. Shame level after an episode. 1 means minimal shame. 10 means intense self-hatred. Where are you?
Number four. Hiding behavior. 1 means you are open about your eating patterns. 10 means complete secrecy. Where are you?
Number five. Weekend structure. 1 means completely unstructured and isolated. 10 means full of planned activities and connection. Where are you?
Number six. Self-worth as it relates to this pattern. 1 means you feel broken and worthless. 10 means your self-worth is unaffected by eating behavior. Where are you?
Good. I am recording all six. We revisit these at Session 3 and again at graduation.
[--- THEORY OF MIND FOR BINGE EATING (10 min) ---]
Now let me explain what is actually happening in your brain when the switch flips. Once you understand this, the shame starts to dissolve on its own.

Your mind has two operating systems. The conscious mind handles about 12 percent of your processing. It is where your logic lives, your plans, your knowledge of nutrition, your intention to eat normally. It is the part of you that swears after every binge that it will never happen again.
The subconscious mind handles the other 88 percent. It runs your automatic behaviors, your emotional responses, your survival programs. And it runs the binge pattern.

At some point, your subconscious learned a survival equation. Overwhelming pressure plus no available escape equals emergency protocol: consume food rapidly, flood the system with dopamine, achieve temporary numbness, survive the moment. That equation was installed through repetition. Hundreds of cycles. Now it runs automatically.

The switch you describe is the moment the 12 percent goes offline and the 88 percent takes over. It feels instantaneous because the subconscious operates below awareness. By the time you realize what is happening, the food is already ordered.

Here is the chemistry. A binge creates a massive dopamine spike. Far larger than a normal meal. Your brain has become accustomed to that spike. Normal meals feel flat. After the binge, dopamine crashes and cortisol floods in. That is the shame. And cortisol is itself a trigger for the subconscious to seek dopamine relief. The shame does not prevent the next binge. It primes it.

And the restriction trap. When you skip meals to compensate, your body registers a caloric deficit. Ghrelin spikes. Leptin drops. Your biology is now primed for the next binge. The punishment creates the vulnerability. That is why the restrict-binge cycle never breaks through willpower.
We do not fight this with the 12 percent. We update the program in the 88 percent.
[--- THE SPEED BUMP CONCEPT (conscious, pre-trance) ---]
Right now the pattern runs: pressure builds, threshold reached, switch flips, binge activates. No gap. No pause. No choice point.
What we install today is a speed bump in the 10-second window before the switch. The new pattern: pressure builds, threshold approaches, speed bump engages, you become aware, you choose.

The speed bump is a physical sensation paired with a question. The sensation is heaviness in your hands. When the pre-binge feeling arrives, your hands get heavy. Noticeably heavy. That heaviness is the speed bump firing.
In that awareness, one question rises from the subconscious. Not from willpower. From the deeper mind: Do I want to feel the way I felt last time, 30 minutes from now?
That question creates a space. And in that space, three new doors: Move. Connect. Create. Any of those changes your neurochemistry without the binge, without the crash, without the shame.
[--- SUGGESTIBILITY TEST ---]

Before the hypnosis, I want to run a brief exercise that shows me how your subconscious processes suggestions. This tells me whether your mind responds best to direct instruction or indirect imagery so I can calibrate everything in trance to your specific operating style.
[[Run standard EP test. For Marcus (54% Physical, Kinesthetic), arm rigidity or hand clasp resonates. Kinesthetic VAK means body-sensation language. Note: balanced EP may shift under trance.]]
[--- INDUCTION: ARM-RAISING ---]
[HYBRID APPROACH: 54% Physical -- lead direct, layer inferential]
Sit comfortably. Both feet flat on the floor. Hands on your thighs, palms down. If you are wearing glasses, take them off now.
Raise your right arm and bend it at the elbow. Place the palm of your hand in front of your face, about ten inches away, fingers pointing up, above your eye level.
Stare at your middle finger. Focus on it. Take a deep breath in. And as you exhale, your fingers are separating. Wider. Further apart. Spreading now.
I am going to ask you a few questions. Do not answer out loud. Just nod yes or no.

Have you ever been so focused on your work that hours passed without you noticing? Have you ever been driving and missed your exit because your mind was somewhere else? Have you ever been reading something and realized you read the same paragraph three times?

Good. Now notice what is happening in your body. Your breathing is slowing. Your muscles are softening. One hand feels heavier against your leg. The other hand is beginning to feel lighter. As if something is drawing it upward and inward.

That lightness is increasing now. Your hand is rising. Moving closer to your face. Your head may begin to tilt forward. Allow that movement. Whether your hand rises to your face or your head comes down to your hand, let it happen at whatever pace your body chooses.
The moment your hand touches your forehead, give me a nod. At that instant you will reach your peak of suggestibility and enter the hypnotic state.
[Wait for contact and nod.] Deep Sleep.

Each and every time I suggest the words Deep Sleep to you, for the purpose of hypnosis and with your permission, you will enter this state of hypnosis very quickly, calmly, and deeply, and the physical body will relax.
[--- DEEPENING: 5-0 COUNT + PHS ---]
Now let your hand drift back down to your lap. Settling. Heavy. Still.
As I count from five down to zero, each number takes you deeper.
Five. Going down now. Your body releasing tension you did not know you were carrying.
Four. Deeper. Muscles letting go. Jaw unclenching.
Three. Emotionally settling. The noise fading. The pressure easing.
Two. Deeper still. Mind quieting. Breathing slow and even.
One. Almost there. Sinking into this comfortable, heavy state.
Zero. [Snap.] Deep Sleep.

Each and every time I suggest the words Deep Sleep to you, for the purpose of hypnosis and with your permission, you will enter this state of hypnosis very quickly, calmly, and deeply, and the physical body will relax.
[--- PROGRESSIVE RELAXATION: BODY RECONNECTION ---]

As you rest in this deep state, I want you to reconnect with your body. Your body has been sending signals all day. Signals about hunger. Signals about fullness. Those signals have been drowned out by the speed, the urgency, the pressure. Today we turn the volume back up.
Starting at the top of your head. A wave of warm relaxation flows down. Scalp releases. Forehead softens. Tension around your eyes melts. Jaw lets go completely.
The wave moves through your neck. Shoulders drop. All the weight you have been carrying — the secrets, the shame, the hiding — flows off your shoulders and dissolves.

Down through your chest. Heart rate settling. Breathing deep and automatic. Now bring awareness to your stomach. Settle attention there gently. Your stomach knows exactly when it has had enough. It sends that signal every time. We are turning up the volume on that signal today.
The wave continues through your midsection, hips, legs. Feet pressing into the floor. Every cell releasing. Reconnecting. Remembering what calm feels like.
Five. Four. Three. Two. One. Zero. [Snap.] Deep Sleep.
[Repeat PHS.]
[--- CONTROL ROOM DEEPENER ---]
Now imagine yourself descending a staircase. Ten steps down into the deepest part of your mind.
Ten. Nine. Eight. Descending. Seven. Six. Deeper. Five. Four. Three. Almost there. Two. One.
At the bottom is a door. Behind it, a control room. This is where your automatic programs run. Walk through the door.
Inside you see control panels, switches, dials, screens. And on the far wall, a lever. That lever is the binge switch. You recognize it immediately.
Walk toward it. Right now there is nothing between you and the lever. When pressure builds, the lever gets pulled with nothing to slow it down.
Now look to the right. There is a new installation. A speed bump. A raised platform in the floor in front of the lever. Anyone approaching must slow down to cross it. It cannot be jumped or avoided.
On the speed bump, a question is engraved: Do I want to feel this way in 30 minutes?
That speed bump is being installed permanently. From this moment forward, every time pressure pushes toward the lever, the speed bump activates first.
[--- SPEED BUMP INSTALLATION (in trance) ---]
Now imagine a scene. Friday evening. Your apartment. Work is done. The apartment is quiet. You feel it building. That familiar pressure. The pull toward food.
The old pattern is trying to fire. The switch is warming up.
But now, as pressure approaches the threshold, the speed bump engages. Your hands get heavy. Noticeably heavy. That heaviness is the signal. You are aware.
The question rises: Do I want to feel the way I felt last time, 30 minutes from now?
You pause. The switch has not flipped. The phone is in your hand but the order has not been placed. There is a window. Five seconds. Ten seconds.

Three doors appear. Move. Connect. Create. You choose one. Maybe you stand up and walk. Ten minutes around the block. Maybe you call someone. Maybe you open your laptop and code something that matters.
As you walk through the new door, the pressure dissipates. Not because you fought it. Because you rerouted it. The switch did not flip. The speed bump held.
This speed bump is installing itself in your subconscious now. Permanent. Automatic. It fires every time the pre-binge pressure arrives. You do not have to remember it. You do not have to will it.

And the shame dissolution begins now. When shame arrives after eating, you recognize it for what it is. A feeling. Not a fact. Not your identity. Shame arrives, and you meet it with one thought: that was the old program. It does not define me. It has less power every single time.

These suggestions grow stronger day by day. Stronger by the hour. Stronger by the minute. The speed bump is in place. The shame dissolution is active. The new doors are available. All firmly embedded in your subconscious mind. They belong to you.
[--- COUNT OUT + HOMEWORK ---]
Now I am going to count from zero up to five. With each number you become more alert, more awake, more grounded.

Zero. Sealing every suggestion into the subconscious. The Speed Bump is installed. The Shame Dissolution is active. The three doors are in place. Sealing in the new program. Sealing out the old automatic cycle.
One. Slowly and calmly beginning to come up.
Two. Becoming more physically aware. More mentally alert. Knowing that tonight, this weekend, the speed bump is in place.
Three. Coming up higher. Feeling solid. Feeling grounded. Feeling something you may not have felt in a long time: hope that this can actually change.
Four. Eyes beginning to open.
Five. Eyes open. Wide awake. Fully alert, refreshed, and steady. Welcome back.
One, two, three, four, five. Eyes open, wide awake.
[--- POST-SESSION: HOMEWORK ASSIGNMENT ---]
Before you leave, three things for the week.

First. Keep a binge journal. Every time the pre-binge feeling arrives, write down: date and time, trigger, what you felt in the 10 seconds before, whether the speed bump engaged, what you did, and how you felt afterward. Not judgment. Mapping.
Second. No restriction. If a binge happens, you eat three normal meals the next day anyway. No skipping. No punishing gym sessions. Restriction primes the next binge. We break that link today.

Third. When the pre-binge feeling arrives, notice the heaviness in your hands. That is the speed bump. Try one of the three doors: move, connect, or create. Ten minutes. If the binge still happens after, that is acceptable. The goal is one speed bump. One interrupted moment proves the window exists.
[[Schedule Session 2 within 1-2 weeks. Prioritize early in the week so Marcus has support before the weekend.]]

One last thing. If you have a binge episode this week, do not call yourself a failure. The speed bump is new. It may not catch every trigger immediately. What matters is that it caught one. One pause, even for a second, is evidence the program is running. And it gets stronger every day.
I will see you at Session 2.
[=== POST-SESSION THERAPIST CHECKLIST ===]

[[1. Record all 6 SMART baselines. 2. Confirm BED screening status — if pattern meets DSM-5 criteria, note for referral discussion. 3. Note specific pre-binge somatic indicators (speed bump trigger). 4. Note EP confirmation or shift. 5. Record verbatim answer to normal-eating question (treatment frame). 6. Assess restriction pattern severity. 7. Note hiding behavior specifics. 8. Plan Session 2: shame dissolution and restrict-binge cycle. 9. Send AVS within 24 hours.]]

cases.title: Stress Eating: The Cortisol-Craving Connection
cases.presenting: I eat perfectly until about three in the afternoon. Then the stress from work hits and I start snacking. Vending machine. Office candy. Drive-through on the way home. I know exactly when it happens and I still cannot stop it. My doctor told me if I do not lose weight I will be on metformin within a year. I am pre-diabetic. I have two teenagers I am telling to eat healthy while I am hiding fast food wrappers in my car. I am a hospital administrator. I manage four hundred people. But I cannot manage what I put in my mouth after three PM.

client.name: Priya K.
client.history: Stress-driven eating pattern. High-pressure job managing hospital operations with 12-hour days. Eats well until 3 PM, then stress builds and snacking begins. Vending machine, office candy, drive-through on the way home. Weight gain primarily around midsection (cortisol distribution pattern). Has tried meal prep — works for 2 weeks then collapses under work pressure. Sleeps 5 hours per night. Married, two teenagers. Feels guilty eating in front of family because she tells them to eat healthy. BMI 29. Pre-diabetic (A1C 5.9). Doctor warned: if you do not lose weight, you will be on metformin within a year.

intake_dialogue.text: Priya, tell me about the eating pattern that concerns you. Not the nutrition details. Tell me about the experience. When does it start, what does it feel like, and what happens?

It is like clockwork. I am fine in the morning. I eat a healthy breakfast. I have my salad at lunch. I am disciplined. I run a hospital. I manage four hundred employees. I handle crises all day long. But around three in the afternoon, something shifts. The stress from the day starts piling up. My shoulders tighten. My head starts pounding. And I reach for food. The vending machine. The candy jar on my assistant's desk. Whatever is fastest. By the time I leave work at seven, I have already eaten five hundred extra calories in snacks. And then I hit the drive-through on the way home because I am too exhausted to cook.

So the morning version of you and the afternoon version of you are running different programs. The morning version has structure, energy, and willpower. The afternoon version has depleted all of those resources managing four hundred people and a hospital full of emergencies. And when the resources run out, the body reaches for the fastest fuel it can find.

That is exactly it. By three PM I have made a thousand decisions. I am running on caffeine and adrenaline. And when the adrenaline fades, I crash. My body screams for sugar. For salt. For anything that will give me ten minutes of relief. I know it is stress eating. I can name it while I am doing it. But I cannot stop it.

Priya, naming it while doing it is actually important. It tells me your conscious mind is fully aware of the pattern. The problem is not awareness. The problem is that awareness alone cannot override the cortisol demand. Your body is in a genuine biochemical state by three PM. Cortisol is elevated. Ghrelin, the hunger hormone, is spiking. Leptin, the fullness hormone, is suppressed. Your body is not lying to you. It genuinely believes it needs fuel. The question is what kind of fuel and whether the signal is about hunger or about stress.

It is about stress. I know it is. Because on weekends when I am not at work, I eat normally. I do not crave the vending machine at three PM on a Saturday. It is only when the pressure is on. But here is the worst part. My doctor told me I am pre-diabetic. A1C of 5.9. He said if I do not lose weight I will be on metformin within a year. And I went home and stress-ate about THAT. I ate about the news that my eating is going to give me diabetes.

That is the cycle revealing itself perfectly. Stress creates eating. Eating creates health consequences. Health consequences create more stress. More stress creates more eating. The engine runs on its own fuel. And the guilt adds another layer. Tell me about the family piece.

That is the part that kills me. I have two teenagers. I tell them to eat healthy. I cook dinner most nights. But they see me snacking. They see the drive-through bags. My daughter said to me last month, Mom, you tell us not to eat junk food but you do it every day. I did not have an answer. I just felt ashamed. I am a hypocrite. I manage a hospital but I cannot manage my own health.

Let me stop you there. You are not a hypocrite. A hypocrite chooses to do the wrong thing. You are not choosing. You are running a stress-response program that overrides your choices by three PM every day. That is a very different thing. And the fact that you care so deeply about what your daughter sees tells me your values are perfectly intact. The program is the problem, not the person.

I just want to get through the afternoon without reaching for food I do not need. I want to come home and cook dinner and eat with my family and not feel guilty about what I already consumed on the way home. I want my A1C to come down so my doctor stops looking at me like I am a ticking time bomb. I want to practice what I preach to my kids.

clinical_notes.theory_of_mind: Stress eating in this client is a cortisol-mediated subconscious program. The 88 percent has learned that when cortisol elevation reaches a threshold (approximately 3 PM, after 7-8 hours of high-pressure decision-making), the fastest relief is high-calorie food consumption. The conscious 12 percent has full awareness of the pattern — Priya can name it in real time — but awareness without subconscious reprogramming is insufficient because the cortisol-ghrelin cascade is biochemical, not cognitive. The morning discipline is not willpower — it is the absence of the cortisol trigger. By afternoon, decision fatigue has depleted prefrontal cortex resources, cortisol is elevated from sustained stress, and the subconscious defaults to its most efficient relief protocol: eat. The drive-through on the way home is a second-stage trigger: exhaustion plus transition from work identity to home identity. The family guilt layer adds shame-based cortisol on top of stress-based cortisol, amplifying the next day's cycle.
clinical_notes.ep_approach: 71% Emotional — strongly Emotional-lane. Use permissive, imagery-rich, inferential delivery throughout. You may notice, you might find, allowing yourself to. Metaphor-heavy: the stress as a volume dial, the body as a wise advisor being drowned out by noise, the afternoon as a bridge between two versions of yourself. Avoid direct commands about not eating or stopping — the Emotional subconscious will resist prohibition. Instead, install alternatives and let the subconscious choose. Auditory VAK: emphasize sound-based language. Listen to your body. Hear the signal. The quiet voice beneath the noise. The sound of your own breathing replacing the craving. Priya processes through what she hears, not what she sees or feels.
clinical_notes.key_reframe: Your body is not betraying you. It is doing exactly what cortisol tells it to do. When cortisol rises, ghrelin rises, leptin drops, and the body demands high-calorie fuel. That is biology, not weakness. We do not fight the biology. We change what your body reaches for when the stress signal fires. We redirect the 3 PM response from the vending machine to something that actually lowers cortisol instead of just masking it temporarily.
clinical_notes.contraindications: Pre-diabetic (A1C 5.9). MUST coordinate with physician. DO NOT promise blood sugar improvement, A1C reduction, or any medical outcome — that is medical territory. Hypnotherapy addresses the behavioral and emotional drivers of stress eating; medical monitoring remains with her physician. Screen for burnout or clinical depression — 12-hour days, 5 hours of sleep, chronic stress, and guilt are burnout indicators. Screen for sleep disorders — 5 hours per night is below clinical minimum and directly drives cortisol dysregulation and appetite hormone disruption. If sleep deprivation is primary, address sleep as a prerequisite to sustainable eating change. Screen for thyroid dysfunction (weight gain around midsection, fatigue). Screen for anxiety disorder (the stress response may be clinical, not just situational).
clinical_notes.root_cause_assessment: Occupational stress with no decompression. The hospital administrator role provides constant high-stakes decision-making with minimal recovery. The 12-hour day leaves no margin for stress processing, so the body processes it through food. Sleep deprivation (5 hours) dysregulates cortisol rhythm — cortisol should drop in the evening but chronic sleep debt keeps it elevated, driving evening cravings. The caregiver identity (managing 400 people, raising 2 teenagers, cooking dinner, being the responsible one) means Priya gives constantly and receives little. Food is the one thing she does for herself. The guilt about eating in front of the family suggests a perfectionist identity — she must model perfect behavior, and any deviation is experienced as moral failure. Childhood exploration: was food restricted in childhood? Was there a cultural association between feeding others and love? Was self-sacrifice valorized?
clinical_notes.neurochemistry: Cortisol elevation drives increased ghrelin (hunger hormone) and decreased leptin (fullness hormone), creating cravings specifically for sugar, fat, and salt — the exact foods available in vending machines and drive-throughs. This is biological, not moral. Cortisol also promotes visceral fat storage around the midsection, which itself produces inflammatory cytokines that further elevate cortisol — a metabolic vicious cycle. The 5-hour sleep pattern compounds the problem: sleep deprivation increases cortisol by 37 to 45 percent the following day, elevates ghrelin by 28 percent, and reduces leptin by 18 percent. The client is biochemically primed for overeating before she walks into the office. Breaking the cycle requires: (1) stress response modification (redirect the 3 PM cortisol spike), (2) cortisol management techniques (breathing, movement, micro-recovery), (3) sleep improvement (even 30 minutes more per night measurably reduces next-day cortisol), and (4) elimination of the guilt layer that adds shame-cortisol on top of stress-cortisol.
clinical_notes.evidence_base: Stradling 1998 (Oxford): hypnotherapy combined with stress reduction maintained weight loss at 18-month follow-up. Kirsch 1995 meta-analysis: CBT plus hypnosis outperformed CBT alone, benefits tripling post-treatment. Daubenmier 2011: mindfulness-based stress eating intervention reduced cortisol awakening response, which correlated with reduced abdominal fat. Epel 2001: cortisol reactivity directly predicted greater caloric intake after stress exposure, confirming the cortisol-craving mechanism. Van Cauter 1999: sleep restriction to 4 hours increased ghrelin 28 percent and decreased leptin 18 percent. The evidence supports addressing stress physiology and sleep as prerequisites to sustainable eating change.

therapy: Stress Response Redirect: the core intervention. When cortisol rises at 3 PM, the current response is eat. The new response is a 90-second micro-recovery: three deep breaths (activates parasympathetic, drops cortisol), stand up and move for 60 seconds (metabolizes cortisol through movement), then ask: am I hungry or am I stressed? 3 PM Protocol: a pre-emptive intervention installed before the crash. At 2:45 PM every day, before the stress threshold is reached, a 5-minute reset activates. Stand up. Walk to the window or the door. Three deep breaths. A planned healthy snack (protein and fat, not sugar — stabilizes blood sugar without the spike-crash). This protocol intercepts the cortisol wave before it peaks, reducing the amplitude of the craving that follows.

Drive-Through Bypass: the drive-through on the way home is a conditioned environmental trigger. Install a new route home that does not pass the fast food locations. Place a prepared snack in the car (nuts, fruit, protein bar) that satisfies the transition-hunger without the guilt. The car becomes a recovery space, not a feeding space. Two minutes of breathing in the parked car before driving home resets the nervous system for the transition from work to home.

Cortisol Dial: similar to the Depth Dial concept but applied to stress. In the control room of the subconscious, there is a dial marked STRESS. Right now it is pinned at 8 or 9 by 3 PM every day. In trance, Priya learns to reach for that dial. Three breaths, and the dial turns down one notch. Movement, and the dial turns down another. The dial does not need to reach zero. It needs to come down below the threshold where the craving fires. From 8 to 5 is enough. The craving does not fire at 5.

Sleep Connection: more sleep equals less cortisol equals fewer cravings. This is not a suggestion — it is biochemistry. Even 30 additional minutes of sleep per night measurably reduces the next day's cortisol response. Install the sleep priority: the body deserves rest. Rest is not laziness. Rest is the foundation that makes every other change possible. One episode of improved sleep creates a cascade of hormonal improvements that make the next afternoon easier.

Family Alignment: instead of eating separately and hiding drive-through bags, eat WITH the family. The family dinner becomes the evening anchor. Priya does not need to eat differently from her children. She needs to eat the same meal, at the same table, at the same time. The modeling is not about perfection — it is about presence. When her daughter sees her mother choosing food consciously, sitting down, eating slowly, that IS the lesson. The guilt dissolves when the behavior aligns with the values.
