session_script: [=== SESSION 1: INTAKE, ASSESSMENT, AND STRESS RESPONSE REDIRECT ===]
[--- WARM-UP AND RAPPORT (5 min) ---]

Priya, welcome. Thank you for being here. I know how much you have on your plate, no pun intended, and carving out this time tells me you are serious about making a change. Before we start, I want to be clear about something. This is not a diet program. I am not going to tell you what to eat or give you a meal plan. What we are going to do is change the automatic program that drives the eating pattern you described. The part that fires before you can think about it.

Here is how today works. First, we talk. I am going to ask you about the eating pattern, the stress, the timing, the family piece. Then I will explain the neuroscience behind what is happening in your brain at three in the afternoon and why knowing it is stress eating has not been enough to stop it. After that, we do hypnosis. You will leave today with a new response installed in your subconscious that activates the next time the three PM stress signal fires. Sound good?
[--- L.O.V.E. INTAKE: LISTEN, OBSERVE, VERIFY, EMPATHIZE (15 min) ---]
[L: LISTEN -- open-ended exploration]
Tell me about the eating pattern that brought you here. Not what you eat. Tell me what happens. When does it start, what does it feel like, and how does the rest of the day unfold?

[[Listen for: the 3 PM threshold, the cortisol-craving connection, the decision fatigue, the drive-through habit, the family guilt, the pre-diabetic diagnosis. Watch for: shoulder tension in the chair (she carries stress physically), voice speeding up when describing work (activation), voice dropping when discussing guilt and the daughter's comment (shame).]]
[O: OBSERVE -- reflect the pattern]

I notice something in what you just described. You have two completely different relationships with food depending on the time of day. Morning Priya is disciplined, structured, in control. Afternoon Priya is running on fumes, cortisol, and whatever the vending machine has. Those are not two different levels of willpower. Those are two different biochemical states. And we are going to address the biochemistry, not the willpower.
[V: VERIFY -- map the specifics]
Walk me through a typical workday from breakfast to bedtime. What do you eat, when, and what is your stress level at each point?

[[Map the full timeline: breakfast (healthy, low stress), lunch (healthy, moderate stress), 2-3 PM (stress building, no food yet), 3 PM (threshold, snacking begins), 3-7 PM (continuous grazing, 500+ extra calories), 7 PM (drive-through on the way home), dinner with family (guilt, performs normalcy). Identify the exact moment the pattern activates.]]
What is happening at work around three PM? What makes that specific hour the breaking point?
[[Expected: accumulated decisions, crises from the morning catching up, fatigue, caffeine wearing off, meetings back-to-back.]]
Tell me about the drive-through. What do you order? And what happens in the car?
[[The car is a private space — similar to Marcus's apartment. Eating in the car is hidden eating. The family does not see the drive-through bags.]]
How much sleep are you getting? And what time do you finally get to bed?
[E: EMPATHIZE -- validate and reframe]

Priya, I want you to hear this. You are not a hypocrite. You are not weak. You manage a hospital. You raise two teenagers. You cook dinner. You hold everything together for everyone around you. And by three PM, your brain has used up its reserves. Every decision you made from seven in the morning to three in the afternoon depleted the same neurological resource pool. By the time the vending machine calls, there is nothing left in the tank to say no with. That is not a character flaw. That is resource depletion. And it has a biochemical solution.
[--- STRESS-EATING PATTERN ANALYSIS (5 min) ---]

Let me explain what is happening in your body at three PM. Cortisol is your stress hormone. It has been elevated since you walked into the hospital at seven AM. By three PM it is at peak levels. When cortisol stays elevated, it triggers two hormonal changes. Ghrelin, the hunger hormone, goes up. Leptin, the fullness hormone, goes down. Your body is chemically demanding high-calorie food. Sugar. Salt. Fat. It is not asking. It is demanding.
This is not about discipline. This is about chemistry. Your body is not betraying you. It is responding to cortisol exactly the way it is designed to respond.

And then the sleep factor. Five hours. Your body needs seven to eight to properly regulate cortisol rhythm. On five hours, tomorrow's cortisol starts higher and the afternoon crash comes earlier. Every night of short sleep makes the next afternoon harder.

Now here is the question that changes everything. If you could not change your weight or your A1C through this process, but you could change your response to stress so that food is no longer what your body reaches for at three PM, would that be worth doing?
[[Record the answer. This is the treatment frame. Expected: yes, because the stress eating is destroying my health and my relationship with my kids' eating habits.]]
[--- SMART BASELINES (5 min) ---]
I need six baseline numbers. All on a 1-to-10 scale. These are not judgments. They are starting coordinates.
Number one. Stress eating frequency. 1 means it rarely happens. 10 means it happens every workday. Where are you?
Number two. Control over the 3 PM snacking. 1 means zero control, it happens automatically. 10 means you always choose consciously. Where are you?
Number three. Drive-through frequency. How many days per week do you hit the drive-through on the way home? Convert that to a 1-to-10 scale.
Number four. Sleep adequacy. 1 means severely sleep-deprived. 10 means consistently well-rested. Where are you?
Number five. Awareness of when stress is driving eating versus genuine hunger. 1 means you cannot tell the difference in the moment. 10 means you always know. Where are you?
Number six. Consistency of eating dinner with your family without guilt or hidden food. 1 means rarely. 10 means every night, fully present, no guilt. Where are you?
Good. All six recorded. We revisit at Session 3 and at graduation.
[--- THEORY OF MIND FOR STRESS EATING (10 min) ---]
Let me explain how your mind processes the stress-eating pattern so you understand exactly what we are changing today.

Your mind has two systems. The conscious mind handles about 12 percent of your processing. It knows the snacking is unnecessary. It knows the drive-through is not helping. It knows the A1C is dangerous. But it has been overworked all day making decisions for four hundred people. By three PM it is running on fumes.

The subconscious mind handles the other 88 percent. It runs your automatic responses. And it has learned a very simple equation through thousands of repetitions: cortisol rises, eat something, cortisol drops temporarily, crisis averted. The subconscious does not care about A1C or calories or what your daughter thinks. It cares about one thing: reducing the immediate threat signal. And food works. Temporarily.

The problem is the temporarily part. The food reduces cortisol for about twenty minutes. Then cortisol rebounds, often higher than before, especially when guilt is added. So the body reaches for more food. That is the three-to-seven-PM grazing pattern. It is not one decision to snack. It is a cortisol loop running on repeat for four hours.

We break this loop not by fighting it with the depleted 12 percent but by installing a new automatic response in the 88 percent. When cortisol rises at three PM, instead of reaching for food, the body reaches for a 90-second micro-recovery that actually lowers cortisol instead of just masking it.
[--- THE MICRO-RECOVERY CONCEPT (conscious, pre-trance) ---]
The current pattern: stress rises, eat, temporary relief, stress returns, eat more. A loop.
The new pattern: stress rises, micro-recovery activates, cortisol actually drops, the craving does not fire.

The micro-recovery takes 90 seconds. Three deep breaths, each one longer than the last. This activates the parasympathetic nervous system, which directly opposes cortisol. Then 60 seconds of movement. Standing up, walking to the window, stretching. Movement metabolizes cortisol through the muscles. Then one question from the subconscious: Am I hungry, or am I stressed?
If hungry, you eat something you chose that morning. A planned snack. Protein and fat, not sugar. It stabilizes blood sugar without the spike-and-crash that drives the next craving.
If stressed, the micro-recovery has already begun lowering cortisol. The craving fades. Not because you fought it. Because you resolved the signal it was responding to.
[--- SUGGESTIBILITY TEST ---]

Before we begin the hypnosis, I want to do a brief exercise that shows me how your subconscious processes information. This tells me the best way to deliver suggestions during trance so they land most effectively for your specific mind.

[[Run standard EP test. For Priya (71% Emotional, Auditory), the lemon visualization with auditory emphasis works well. Note the Auditory VAK — she processes through what she hears, so verbal/sound-based tests and suggestions will be most effective.]]
[--- INDUCTION: ARM-RAISING ---]
[EMOTIONAL LANE: 71% Emotional, Auditory VAK]
I would like you to sit comfortably. Both feet flat on the floor. Hands resting on your thighs, palms down. If you are wearing glasses, you may remove them now.
Good. Now raise your right arm and bend it at the elbow, placing the palm of your hand in front of your face, about ten inches away, with your fingers pointing upward and above eye level.

Stare at your middle finger. Take a deep, comfortable breath in. And as you exhale slowly, you may notice that your fingers are beginning to separate. Gently. Gradually. Wider and wider apart, as if something invisible is softly pushing them apart.
I am going to ask you a few questions. Rather than answering out loud, simply nod your head yes or no.

Have you ever been listening to music and become so absorbed that you forgot where you were? Have you ever been on the phone and someone had to tap your shoulder twice to get your attention? Have you ever been driving home and arrived without remembering the last few turns?

Good. Now listen to my voice and notice what is happening in your body. Your breathing is beginning to slow. You can hear each breath becoming deeper, longer, more relaxed. Your eyelids may begin to flutter. That gentle movement is a natural sign that you are entering the first stages of hypnosis.

You may notice that one hand feels heavier against your leg, while the other, the one in front of you, is beginning to feel lighter. As if something gentle is lifting it. Drawing it inward. When you notice that difference, nod yes.
That lightness is growing. Your hand is drifting closer to your face. Your head may begin to tilt forward to meet it. Allow that movement to happen at whatever pace feels natural and right for you.
The moment your hand touches your forehead, give me a nod. At that instant you will reach your peak of suggestibility and enter the hypnotic state.
[Wait for contact and nod.] Deep Sleep.

Each and every time I suggest the words Deep Sleep to you, for the purpose of hypnosis and with your permission, you will enter this state of hypnosis very quickly, calmly, and deeply, and the physical body will relax.
[--- DEEPENING: 5-0 COUNT + PHS ---]
Now you can gently allow your hand to float back down and rest comfortably on your lap.
As I count from five down to zero, each number will take you deeper into this peaceful, comfortable state.
Five. Going down now. Deeper and deeper. Listen to the sound of my voice and let everything else fade.
Four. Your body softening. Your shoulders dropping. That tension you carry from seven AM to seven PM is melting away.
Three. Emotionally calm. Peaceful. The four hundred people, the decisions, the crises — all of it is outside this room. In here, there is only quiet.
Two. Mentally settling. The noise of the day dissolving. Your breathing slow, deep, even.
One. Deeper still. Drifting down into the most comfortable, safe, quiet space.
Zero. [Snap.] Deep Sleep.

Each and every time I suggest the words Deep Sleep to you, for the purpose of hypnosis and with your permission, you will enter this state of hypnosis very quickly, calmly, and deeply, and the physical body will relax.
[--- PROGRESSIVE RELAXATION: STRESS RELEASE ---]

Now as you rest in this deep, comfortable state, I want to guide your attention through your body. You carry stress in your body all day long. Your body has been waiting for permission to let it go. This is that permission.
Starting at the top of your head. A warm wave of release begins to flow downward. Your scalp softens. Your forehead smooths. The lines of concentration that have been etched there all day dissolve.
The wave moves to your eyes. They have been scanning, assessing, managing all day. Now they rest. Your jaw unclenches. You may not have realized how tightly you were holding it. Let it go completely.

Now your neck. Your shoulders. This is where you carry it all. The responsibility. The decisions. The weight of four hundred people who depend on you. Feel that weight lifting off your shoulders now. Not because the responsibility is gone. Because in this moment, you do not have to carry it. Someone else is holding it for you. You are allowed to put it down.

Down through your chest. Your heart rate settling into a calm, steady rhythm. Your breathing deep and automatic. Now bring your awareness to your stomach. Listen to it. Not with your ears. With your attention. Your stomach has been sending signals all day. Hungry. Not hungry. Full. Stressed. Those signals have been drowned out by the noise of the hospital, the decisions, the pressure. Right now, in this quiet space, you can hear the signals clearly. The body knows the difference between hunger and stress. We are restoring that signal today.

The warm wave continues through your midsection, your hips, your legs, your feet. Every cell releasing. Every muscle softening. Your entire body settling into the deepest rest it has had in weeks. Perhaps months.
Five. Four. Three. Two. One. Zero. [Snap.] Deep Sleep.
[Repeat PHS.]
[--- GARDEN PATHWAY DEEPENER ---]

Now imagine you are walking down a long hospital corridor. It is quiet. The fluorescent lights are behind you. The noise of the day is behind you. With each step the corridor becomes warmer, softer, more natural.
At the end of the corridor is a door. Not a hospital door. A garden door. Wooden. Warm. Inviting. Push it open and step through.

On the other side is a garden. Quiet. Beautiful. Sunlight filtering through leaves. You can hear birds. You can hear water running somewhere nearby. You can hear the wind moving through the trees. Listen to those sounds. They are the opposite of the hospital. No alarms. No pages. No phones. No decisions required. Just this garden and the sound of calm.

Walk deeper into the garden. With each step you go deeper into hypnosis. There is a bench. Sit down. Feel the warmth of the sun on your skin. Feel the ground solid beneath your feet. This garden is your sanctuary. It lives inside you. And you can return here in seconds whenever you need to.
[--- STRESS RESPONSE REDIRECT INSTALLATION (in trance) ---]

Now I want you to imagine a scene. It is three o'clock in the afternoon. You are at your desk. The morning has been relentless. Decision after decision. Crisis after crisis. Your shoulders are tight. Your head is beginning to pound. And you feel it — that familiar pull. The vending machine. The candy jar. Something, anything, to take the edge off.

But this time, something is different. Before the hand reaches for the drawer, before the feet carry you to the vending machine, something activates. A quiet signal from your subconscious. Not willpower. Something deeper. Something automatic.

You take a breath. One deep breath in through the nose. Hold it for a moment. Exhale slowly through the mouth, twice as long as the inhale. A second breath. Deeper. Slower. A third breath. And as you exhale that third breath, you may notice something shifting. The shoulders drop a fraction. The jaw loosens. The cortisol is beginning to lower. Not through food. Through breath.

You stand up. You walk to the window. Sixty seconds of movement. Your legs carrying the cortisol out of your bloodstream, metabolizing it through the muscles. The pressure that was at an 8 is already coming down. You can feel it. Like a dial turning. Eight. Seven. Six. Five. And at five, the craving does not fire. The threshold was not reached. The vending machine stays where it is. You do not need it.

Now you ask yourself one question. Am I hungry? Or am I stressed? And you listen. Not to the cortisol. To the stomach. To the body. And the body answers honestly. If hungry, you reach for the snack you brought this morning. Protein. Fuel. Chosen consciously. If stressed, the micro-recovery has already done its work. The craving is a wave that is already passing.

This response is installing itself in your subconscious now. Deeply. Permanently. From this moment forward, every time cortisol rises at three in the afternoon, the micro-recovery activates automatically. You do not have to remember it. It fires on its own. Three breaths. Sixty seconds of movement. One honest question. The vending machine loses its pull because the signal it was answering has already been resolved.

And the Cortisol Dial is available to you now. Whenever stress begins to build, you can reach for that dial in your mind and turn it down. Three breaths, one notch down. Movement, another notch down. You do not need to reach zero. You only need to come below the threshold where the craving fires. And that threshold gets higher every day, because every time the micro-recovery runs successfully, the subconscious learns: this is the new protocol. This is how we handle stress now.

These suggestions grow stronger day by day. Stronger by the hour. Stronger by the minute. The Stress Response Redirect is in place. The Cortisol Dial is available. The micro-recovery is automatic. All firmly embedded in your subconscious mind. And they belong to you. They are yours.
[--- COUNT OUT + HOMEWORK ---]
Now I am going to count from zero up to five. With each number you will become more alert, more awake, more refreshed, with a wonderful feeling of confidence and calm.

Zero. I am closing the door to the subconscious mind, sealing in every suggestion. The Stress Response Redirect is installed. The Cortisol Dial is available. The micro-recovery is automatic. The garden is inside you. Sealing in the new program. Sealing out the old vending-machine reflex.
One. Slowly and calmly beginning to come up.
Two. Becoming more physically aware. More mentally alert. Knowing that this afternoon, when three o'clock arrives, the micro-recovery will be there. Automatic. Effortless.
Three. Coming up higher. Feeling rested in a way you may not have felt in months. Not because you slept. Because you let go.
Four. Your eyes are beginning to open.
Five. Eyes open, wide awake. Fully alert, refreshed, and calm. Welcome back.
One, two, three, four, five. Eyes open, wide awake.
[--- POST-SESSION: HOMEWORK ASSIGNMENT ---]
Before you head back to your hospital, three things for this week.

First. Keep a stress-eating journal. Every time you reach for food between meals, write down: the time, what triggered it, your stress level on a 1-to-10 scale, and what you ate. This is not a guilt journal. It is a pattern map. You are an administrator. You make decisions based on data. This is your data.

Second. Practice the 90-second micro-recovery three times tomorrow. Not just at three PM. Practice it at ten AM, at noon, and at three PM. Get the body familiar with the sequence: three breaths, 60 seconds of movement, one question. By the end of the week, it should feel automatic.

Third. Bring a planned snack to work tomorrow. Protein-based. Nuts, cheese, a protein bar, whatever you enjoy. Put it in your desk drawer. That is your three PM fuel if the body says hungry instead of stressed. Having it there means the vending machine is no longer the only option.
[[Schedule Session 2 within 1-2 weeks. The 3 PM Protocol and drive-through work need to happen before the pattern has time to reassert.]]

One more thing. You mentioned your daughter said you tell them not to eat junk food but you do it every day. I want you to know that what we started today is not just about your health. Every time the micro-recovery fires at three PM and you choose differently, you are rewriting the example your children see. You do not need to be perfect. You need to be changing. And as of today, you are.
I will see you at Session 2.
[=== POST-SESSION THERAPIST CHECKLIST ===]

[[1. Record all 6 SMART baselines. 2. Note the exact 3 PM trigger profile (what happens at work, specific foods, duration of grazing window). 3. Note EP confirmation or shift. 4. Note A1C status (5.9, pre-diabetic) — coordinate with physician, do NOT promise medical outcomes. 5. Note sleep hours (5/night) — this is a critical biochemical driver. 6. Note family dynamics: daughter's comment, guilt about modeling. 7. Note drive-through specifics: which route, which restaurants, what is ordered. 8. Assess for burnout indicators (12-hour days, chronic stress, sleep deprivation, guilt). 9. Plan Session 2: 3 PM Protocol installation, Cortisol Dial practice, drive-through bypass. 10. Send AVS within 24 hours.]]

cases.title: Late-Night Eating: The Autopilot Kitchen Run
cases.presenting: I eat perfectly during the day. Healthy lunch, good snacks. Then 8 PM hits and it is like someone else takes over. I sit on the couch, turn on Netflix, and before I know it I have eaten half a bag of chips and a block of cheese. I am not even hungry. I just do it.

client.name: Sarah M.
client.history: Eats well during the day. Problem starts at 8 PM. Works from home, alone most evenings. TV plus snacking is the nightly routine: chips, cheese, crackers, wine. Does not feel hungry and knows it is boredom and habit. Has tried no-eating-after-7 rules but breaks them within 3 days. Gained 25 pounds since starting remote work 2 years ago. No emotional trauma. No medical issues. No medications. Exercise: sporadic yoga. Social life decreased since remote work. Single. Describes the pattern as my brain just turns off and my hand keeps reaching into the bag.

intake_dialogue.text: Sarah, tell me about your evenings. Walk me through what happens from dinner until you go to bed.

Dinner is fine. I make something healthy, I eat it, I clean up. Then around 8 PM I move to the couch, turn on Netflix, and that is when the wheels come off. I will grab some chips. Then cheese and crackers. Sometimes a glass of wine. I am not hungry at all. I know I am not hungry. But my hand just keeps going back to the bag.
You said your hand just keeps going back. It sounds like the eating is happening almost without your permission. Like you are watching yourself do it.

That is exactly it. It is like autopilot. I will be three handfuls in before I even register what I am doing. And then I think, why am I eating this? And I keep eating anyway. It is like the decision was already made before I sat down.
When did this pattern start? Was there a specific point where the evening eating became the routine?

When I went remote. Two years ago. Before that I would come home from the office, maybe go out with friends, go to a class. My evenings had variety. Now every night is the same. Work ends, I close the laptop, I make dinner, and then it is just me and the TV for four hours. The snacking filled the gap. And now I cannot stop.
So the remote work removed the variety, and eating stepped in to fill the empty space in the evening. What about the weekends? Does the same pattern happen?

Less so. If I am out with friends or doing something, I do not think about food at all. It is really only when I am home alone at night. That is the trigger. The couch, the TV, the silence. If I am busy or with people, I am fine.

That tells us something important. The eating is not about food. It is about what happens when the stimulation stops and you are alone with quiet. The food fills a gap that used to be filled by activity and connection.
I never thought about it that way. I always just blamed myself for having no willpower. But you are right. When I am engaged in something, food does not even cross my mind.

Willpower is not the issue here. Your conscious mind already knows you are not hungry. The problem is that your subconscious has built a sequence. Couch plus screen plus evening equals eat. That sequence runs automatically. We do not fight it with willpower. We reprogram the sequence itself.
That would be amazing. Because every rule I set for myself lasts about three days and then I am right back on the couch with the chips. I need something that actually sticks.

Rules engage the 12 percent of your mind that handles conscious decision-making. The eating pattern lives in the other 88 percent. We are going to install the change where the pattern actually lives. That is why it sticks.
Okay. I am ready. What do we do?

clinical_notes.theory_of_mind: This is a pure association-driven habit case. The subconscious has encoded a stimulus chain: couch plus screen plus evening equals eat. The 88 percent runs this sequence automatically without consulting the conscious mind. There is no deep emotional wound, no trauma, no complex root cause. The pattern formed through two years of nightly repetition in a low-stimulation environment. Remote work removed evening variety (social outings, classes, commute decompression), and snacking filled the behavioral vacuum. The conscious mind recognizes the pattern clearly but cannot interrupt the automatic loop. This is the simplest weight management case: rewire the association, fill the behavioral gap, restore evening structure.
clinical_notes.ep_approach: 68% Emotional lane approach: permissive, imagery-rich, metaphor-driven. Use you may notice, you might find, allowing yourself to. Visual VAK: paint vivid mental pictures of the kitchen closing, the couch without food, the hands resting still. Use color, light, and scene-based imagery. Avoid direct commands about not eating. The emotional subconscious responds to invitation, not prohibition.
clinical_notes.key_reframe: Your hands are on autopilot. The conscious mind checked out at 8 PM and the subconscious runs the same program: couch, screen, hand to bag, mouth. The sequence has been reinforced thousands of times over two years. We do not fight the sequence. We reprogram the 8 PM transition so the automatic behavior routes somewhere new.
clinical_notes.contraindications: Screen for depression or loneliness masked by routine. Remote work isolation can present as simple boredom but may indicate subclinical depression. Screen for alcohol frequency: wine was mentioned casually but nightly wine plus snacking is a compound habit. Ask about quantity and frequency. If wine is nightly and exceeds one glass, address alcohol as a separate behavioral loop. Screen for social anxiety that may be preventing the client from rebuilding social connections. Low complexity case overall. Good for beginning therapist practice.
clinical_notes.root_cause_assessment: No deep childhood conditioning or trauma driving this pattern. Root cause is environmental and behavioral: the shift to remote work two years ago eliminated evening structure, social contact, and activity variety. The subconscious filled the stimulation gap with the most available dopamine source: food plus screen. The pattern was reinforced nightly for approximately 700 repetitions over two years. The 25-pound weight gain is a downstream consequence, not the cause. Address the environmental gap and the association chain, and the eating resolves.
clinical_notes.neurochemistry: The couch-screen-eat sequence triggers a modest but reliable dopamine loop. Salty and fatty foods (chips, cheese) activate the reward circuit. The screen provides passive stimulation that lowers executive function, making automatic eating easier. The combination of low alertness (passive TV watching) and high accessibility (food within arm's reach) creates optimal conditions for unconscious consumption. Evening cortisol should be declining, but boredom and under-stimulation can produce a restless cortisol bump that the subconscious interprets as eat something. Breaking the physical proximity to food and replacing passive screen time with even mildly engaging activity disrupts the neurochemical conditions that support the habit.
clinical_notes.evidence_base: Habit research (Wood and Neal 2007): behavior repetition in stable contexts creates automaticity. Removing or altering the context cue disrupts the automatic chain. Implementation intentions (Gollwitzer 1999): if-then planning (if 8 PM, then specific alternative activity) significantly outperforms willpower-based restriction. Mindless eating research (Wansink 2006): proximity and visibility of food are stronger predictors of consumption than hunger. Moving food out of sight and arm's reach reduces consumption by 20 to 30 percent without any conscious effort.

session_plan.pretalk_focus: Theory of Mind applied to habits: the 88/12 split. How the subconscious builds automatic sequences through repetition. The couch-screen-eat chain as a program, not a character flaw. Why willpower rules (no eating after 7) fail within days: 12 percent cannot sustain override of 88 percent. The concept of context-dependent automaticity: same couch, same time, same behavior.
session_plan.induction: Arm-raising (standard). Emotional lane (68%): permissive, inferential language throughout. Visual VAK: emphasize imagery, color, light, seeing the change. Warm, inviting tone. Allow the client to build the pictures in her own mind.
deepeners: 5-0 Count with PHS (standard foundation)
Reactional x2-4 (deepen and test depth)
Progressive Relaxation with evening-themed imagery (the body settling into the couch, but differently this time, settling into stillness rather than reaching)
Garden pathway descent (visual, evening garden at dusk, peaceful transition from day to night without food)
therapy: 8 PM Circuit Breaker: the core intervention. At 8 PM, the old sequence fires: couch, screen, eat. We install a new first step. At 8 PM, before sitting down, a brief physical action breaks the chain. Stand in the kitchen. Close the cabinet. Say out loud or silently: the kitchen is closed. This physical ritual interrupts the automatic sequence at its initiation point. The subconscious cannot run the old program because the first domino has been replaced.

Hand Awareness Installation: the hands have been operating on autopilot, reaching into bags and packages without conscious direction. We install a micro-pause in the hands. Before the hand reaches for food in the evening, a momentary awareness activates. The hand pauses. A brief question surfaces: am I reaching because I am hungry, or because this is what my hand always does at this time? That pause, even half a second, breaks the automaticity.

Kitchen Closure Ritual: at 7:30 PM, the client physically closes the kitchen. Wipes the counters. Puts away any visible food. Closes the pantry. Turns off the kitchen light. This is a physical boundary that the subconscious recognizes as a signal: eating time is over. The ritual creates a clean break between the eating part of the evening and the non-eating part. The subconscious respects physical boundaries more than mental rules.

Evening Activity Replacement: the snacking fills a gap. Remove the snacking and the gap remains, which will pull the old behavior back. We must fill the gap with something that provides mild stimulation and engagement. Identify 3 to 5 activities the client genuinely enjoys that are incompatible with eating: drawing or sketching (hands occupied, visual engagement), a walk around the block (change of environment), calling a friend (social connection), a puzzle or craft (tactile engagement), gentle yoga or stretching (body awareness). The client chooses one each evening before sitting on the couch.

Boredom Reframe: boredom is not a problem to be solved with food. Boredom is a signal that the mind is ready for something new. It is an invitation, not an emergency. When boredom arrives in the evening, it means the subconscious is available and open. Feed it engagement, not calories. Boredom becomes a doorway instead of a trigger.

Social Connection Prescription: the pattern intensified when social contact decreased. Evenings with people do not produce the snacking pattern. Rebuilding even two social evenings per week disrupts the nightly routine and reduces the isolation that feeds the habit. This is not therapy. This is environmental design.
session_plan.countout: Standard 0-5 with suggestion seal. Zero seals in every installation: the 8 PM Circuit Breaker, the Hand Awareness pause, the Kitchen Closure ritual, the Evening Activity replacement. All locked into the subconscious, growing stronger every day, every evening, every time the client sits on the couch. Five brings full alertness with a clear picture of tonight: the kitchen closed, the hands still, the evening full of something other than food.

sessions.title: Intake, Assessment, and 8 PM Circuit Breaker
sessions.focus: L.O.V.E. intake for evening eating pattern. Map the couch-screen-eat sequence. Establish 6 SMART baselines (1-10 subjective scales). Theory of Mind for habits. Suggestibility testing. First induction. Install 8 PM Circuit Breaker and Kitchen Closure ritual. Homework: close the kitchen at 7:30 every night this week, log what happens at 8 PM.

sessions.title: Hand Awareness and Evening Replacement
sessions.focus: Review Kitchen Closure compliance and 8 PM logs. Deepen trance. Install Hand Awareness pause. Identify and commit to 3 evening replacement activities. Practice choosing one before sitting on the couch. Homework: choose one replacement activity per evening before TV, continue Kitchen Closure.

sessions.title: Boredom Reframe and Stimulus Control
sessions.focus: Address boredom as the core trigger. Reframe boredom from problem to signal. Install boredom-as-invitation response. Environmental stimulus control: no food visible from the couch, no eating in the living room, designated eating space only. Reinforce Circuit Breaker and Hand Awareness. Homework: when boredom hits, name it out loud and choose an activity from the list.

sessions.title: Social Reconnection and Isolation Processing
sessions.focus: Address the social isolation created by remote work. Process the loss of evening variety and social contact. Install motivation for rebuilding social evenings. Identify 2 to 3 people to reconnect with and specific activities to propose. Homework: schedule at least one social evening this week.

sessions.title: Self-Hypnosis and Pattern Consolidation
sessions.focus: Teach formal self-hypnosis for maintenance. Consolidate all installations in a single deep session: Circuit Breaker, Hand Awareness, Kitchen Closure, Replacement Activities, Boredom Reframe. Stress inoculation: in trance, rehearse a difficult evening (tired, alone, nothing to do) and practice the full response chain. Homework: daily 60-second self-hypnosis before the evening begins.

sessions.title: Graduation and Maintenance Plan
sessions.focus: Final SMART baseline review. Celebrate progress. Reinforce all installations one final time in trance. Install long-term maintenance anchor: a physical gesture (hand on the TV remote, pause before pressing play) that reactivates the Circuit Breaker. Discuss maintenance: self-hypnosis schedule, social evening frequency, when to return for a booster. Graduation: you are not on a diet. You have a new evening. The kitchen closes. The hands are aware. The couch is for rest, not for eating.

late_night_eating_nights.baseline: Late-night eating 5 to 7 nights per week. Eating after 8 PM is the default evening activity. Frequency: 8 out of 10.
late_night_eating_nights.s3: Late-night eating reduced to 2 to 3 nights per week. Kitchen Closure ritual is active most nights. Frequency drops to 4 to 5 out of 10.
late_night_eating_nights.graduation: Late-night eating is rare, 0 to 1 nights per week. The evening no longer revolves around food. Frequency: 1 to 2 out of 10.

awareness_of_autopilot.baseline: Low awareness of automatic eating. Eating happens before conscious registration. Awareness: 2 out of 10.
awareness_of_autopilot.s3: Awareness increases significantly. Client catches the hand reaching and pauses before eating most of the time. Awareness: 6 out of 10.
awareness_of_autopilot.graduation: Autopilot eating is rare. The client is conscious of every reach for food in the evening. Awareness: 8 to 9 out of 10.

evening_activity.baseline: No evening activities beyond TV and snacking. Engagement: 1 out of 10.
evening_activity.s3: Client engages in a replacement activity 3 to 4 evenings per week. Evenings have variety. Engagement: 5 to 6 out of 10.
evening_activity.graduation: Client has a diverse evening routine. Activities are chosen consciously. TV is one option, not the only option. Engagement: 7 to 8 out of 10.

kitchen_closure_compliance.baseline: No evening boundary with food. Kitchen is open and accessible all night. Compliance: 0 out of 10.
kitchen_closure_compliance.s3: Kitchen Closure ritual performed 5 or more nights per week. The boundary feels natural. Compliance: 7 out of 10.
kitchen_closure_compliance.graduation: Kitchen Closure is automatic. The client does not think about it; it is part of the evening transition. Compliance: 9 out of 10.

boredom_tolerance.baseline: Boredom immediately triggers eating. Tolerance for the uncomfortable feeling: 2 out of 10.
boredom_tolerance.s3: Boredom is recognized as a signal, not an emergency. Client can sit with boredom for several minutes before choosing a response. Tolerance: 5 to 6 out of 10.
boredom_tolerance.graduation: Boredom is neutral or even positive. The client sees it as space for choice. Tolerance: 8 out of 10.

social_connection.baseline: Social evenings are rare, maybe 1 per month. Isolation is the default. Connection: 2 out of 10.
social_connection.s3: Social evenings increase to 1 to 2 per week. Client is actively rebuilding connections. Connection: 5 out of 10.
social_connection.graduation: Social life is healthy and sustainable. Evenings include regular connection with others. Connection: 7 to 8 out of 10.

session_script: [=== SESSION 1: INTAKE, ASSESSMENT, AND 8 PM CIRCUIT BREAKER ===]
[--- WARM-UP AND RAPPORT (5 min) ---]

Sarah, welcome. Thank you for coming in today. I want you to know this is a completely safe, relaxed space. There is no judgment here. What we are going to do today is straightforward: we are going to have a conversation about what is happening in your evenings, I am going to explain why it happens in a way that will make immediate sense, and then we are going to install a change directly into the part of your mind that runs the pattern. You will leave today with a new tool that works tonight.
Sound good? Any questions before we begin?
[--- L.O.V.E. INTAKE (15 min) ---]
[L: LISTEN]
Tell me about your evenings. Start from dinner. Walk me through what a typical night looks like from the time you finish eating dinner until you go to bed.

[[Listen for: the specific time the eating starts, the location (couch, TV room), the trigger sequence (close laptop, make dinner, move to couch, turn on TV, reach for food), the specific foods, the duration of the eating, the emotional state before during and after. Watch body language: does she gesture toward her stomach (somatic awareness) or toward her head (cognitive pattern)?]]
[O: OBSERVE]

I notice something in what you described. The daytime eating is completely under control. You make good choices, you eat appropriate amounts, you stop when full. The pattern only activates in a specific context: alone, evening, couch, screen. It is not a food problem. It is a context problem. Does that match your experience?
[V: VERIFY]

Let me confirm the sequence. You finish work. You make dinner. You eat dinner normally. You clean up. Then around 8 PM you move to the couch, turn on the TV, and the snacking begins. Is that the order? Is 8 PM the consistent start time?
And when the snacking is happening, are you hungry? Physically hungry? Stomach signaling that it needs fuel?
How many nights per week does this happen?
What are the go-to foods? What does your hand reach for first?
Does the pattern happen on weekends? What about evenings when you are out with friends or doing something social?
[[Expected: weekends and social evenings are different. This confirms context-dependent automaticity.]]
[E: EMPATHIZE]

Thank you for being so clear about all of that. Here is what I want you to hear. This is not a willpower problem. You have plenty of willpower. Your daytime eating proves it. The issue is that at 8 PM, your subconscious runs a program that your conscious mind did not write and cannot override through rules alone. You have tried rules. They last three days. That is not failure. That is the architecture of the mind working exactly as designed. Rules live in the 12 percent. The eating program lives in the 88 percent. We are going to update the 88 percent today.
[--- SMART BASELINES (5 min) ---]
Before we go further, I want to set six baselines. All on a 1-to-10 scale. Be honest. There are no wrong answers.
Number one. How many nights per week does the late-night eating happen? Scale it: 1 means rarely, 10 means every single night.
Number two. Awareness of the autopilot. When you are eating at night, how aware are you that you are doing it? 1 means you barely notice, 10 means you are fully conscious of every bite.
Number three. How often do you do something other than TV and snacking in the evening? 1 means never, 10 means you have a rich variety of evening activities.
Number four. Kitchen boundary. Do you have any kind of cutoff or boundary around evening eating? 1 means the kitchen is open all night, 10 means you have a firm boundary that holds.

Number five. Boredom tolerance. When you feel bored in the evening, how long can you sit with that feeling before reaching for food? 1 means you reach immediately, 10 means boredom does not drive eating at all.
Number six. Social connection in the evenings. How often are your evenings spent with other people or in social activity? 1 means almost never, 10 means most evenings involve connection.
Good. I am recording all six. We will recheck them at Session 3.
[--- THEORY OF MIND FOR HABITS (10 min) ---]
Now let me explain what is actually happening when you sit on the couch and the eating starts without your permission.

Your mind has two operating systems. The conscious mind handles about 12 percent of your mental processing. It is where your knowledge lives, your intentions, your rules. It is the part that says no eating after 7.
The subconscious handles the other 88 percent. It runs your heartbeat, your breathing, your digestion. And it runs your automatic behaviors. Every habit you have ever built lives in the 88 percent.

Over the past two years, your subconscious has observed the same sequence roughly 700 times. Work ends. Dinner. Couch. TV. Eat. Seven hundred repetitions. That is more than enough for the subconscious to encode it as an automatic program. The sequence now runs without consulting your conscious mind.

That is why the eating starts before you realize it. The subconscious has already initiated the program. By the time your conscious mind notices, your hand is already in the bag. You are not weak. You are witnessing the 88 percent doing its job: running the program it was trained to run.

The good news is that habits built through repetition are the simplest patterns to reprogram. There is no deep emotional wound to process. No trauma to untangle. We just need to interrupt the sequence at its trigger point and install a new first step. Once the first domino changes, the rest of the chain cannot fire.
[--- INDUCTION: ARM-RAISING ---]
Now we are going to begin the hypnosis portion. Sit comfortably with both feet flat on the floor. Place your hands on your thighs, palms down.
Raise your right arm and bend it at the elbow, placing the palm of your hand in front of your face, about ten inches away, with your fingers pointing upward and above eye level.
Good. Focus your eyes on your middle finger. Take a deep, comfortable breath. And as you exhale, you may notice that your fingers begin to drift apart. Gently. Slowly. Wider and wider.
Now I am going to ask you a few questions. Just nod yes or no.

Have you ever been so absorbed in a show that you lost track of time? Have you ever been drawing or designing something and looked up to find an hour had passed without you noticing? Have you ever driven somewhere familiar and arrived without remembering the turns?
Good. Now notice your breathing. It is beginning to slow. Deepen. When you notice this shift, nod yes.
Your eyelids may begin to feel heavy. A gentle fluttering. That is a natural sign that you are entering the first stage of hypnosis. When you notice it, nod yes.
Notice one hand feels heavier against your leg while the other, in front of your face, feels lighter. Lifting. Drifting. Moving closer to your face at whatever pace feels comfortable.
The moment your hand touches your forehead, give me a nod. At that instant you will reach your peak of suggestibility and enter the hypnotic state.
[Wait for contact and nod.] Deep Sleep.

Each and every time I suggest the words Deep Sleep to you, for the purpose of hypnosis and with your permission, you will enter this state of hypnosis very quickly, calmly, and deeply, and the physical body will relax.
[--- DEEPENING: 5-0 COUNT + PHS ---]
Allow your hand to float gently back down to rest on your lap.
As I count from five down to zero, each number takes you deeper.
Five. Going down. Deeper and deeper. The body beginning to release.
Four. Muscles softening. Shoulders dropping. Hands heavy and still.
Three. Emotionally calm. Safe. Peaceful.
Two. The mind quieting. The noise of the day fading away.
One. Deeper still. Drifting comfortably down.
Zero. [Snap.] Deep Sleep.

Each and every time I suggest the words Deep Sleep to you, for the purpose of hypnosis and with your permission, you will enter this state of hypnosis very quickly, calmly, and deeply, and the physical body will relax.
[--- PROGRESSIVE RELAXATION: EVENING SETTLING ---]
Now imagine it is evening. Your workday is done. Dinner is finished. And your body is settling in. Not into the old pattern. Into something new.
A warm wave of relaxation begins at the top of your head. Your scalp softens. Your forehead smooths. The muscles around your eyes release and soften. Your jaw unclenches.

The wave moves through your neck. Your shoulders drop. Down through your arms. And now notice your hands. Pay special attention to your hands. Your fingers. They are still. Resting. Not reaching for anything. Just resting. Warm and heavy and still.

Your chest opens. Breathing deepens. The wave moves through your stomach. Your stomach is calm. Satisfied from dinner. It does not need anything more. It is sending a clear signal: I have had enough. Thank you.
Down through your hips. Your legs. Your feet. Every part of you sinking into comfortable stillness.
Five. Four. Three. Two. One. Zero. [Snap.] Deep Sleep.
[Repeat PHS.]
[--- 8 PM CIRCUIT BREAKER INSTALLATION ---]
Now I want you to see something in your mind. You are at home. It is 7:30 in the evening. Dinner is done. The dishes are clean. And you are standing in your kitchen.

Look around the kitchen. See the counters. The cabinets. The pantry. The refrigerator. This is the space where food lives. And right now, you are going to do something you have never done before. You are going to close the kitchen for the night.

Watch yourself wipe down the counter. One clean sweep. See the surface gleam. Now close the pantry door. Hear the soft click. Close the cabinet. Close the refrigerator. And now, reach for the kitchen light switch. Turn off the light. The kitchen goes dark. Quiet. Closed.

Feel what that feels like. A clean boundary. A line drawn. The kitchen is closed. Not because you are forbidden from eating. You are an adult. You can eat whenever you choose. The kitchen is closed because the body has had enough. Dinner was sufficient. The stomach is satisfied. There is nothing the kitchen can give you right now that your body actually needs.

Now walk to the couch. Sit down. Notice that something is different. The old program tries to fire. Couch. Screen. Eat. But the first domino is missing. The kitchen is closed. The light is off. The sequence cannot complete because the starting condition has changed.

And in the space where the old pattern used to be, there is quiet. There is choice. There is a moment where your hands rest on your lap, still and warm, and a gentle thought rises: what do I actually want to do with this evening?

Maybe you pick up a sketchpad. Your hands love to draw. They are creative hands, designer hands, and they have been wasted on chip bags. Tonight they draw. Or maybe you call a friend. Or you step outside for a short walk in the cool evening air. Or you simply sit with the quiet and discover that the quiet is not empty. It is peaceful.

The 8 PM Circuit Breaker is installing itself in your subconscious right now. From this evening forward, at 8 PM, the old sequence encounters a new first step. Kitchen closed. Hands aware. Choice activated. The automatic program cannot run because the conditions have changed. This is not willpower. This is reprogramming. And it is permanent.

And your hands. Your beautiful, capable hands. From tonight forward, before they reach for food in the evening, a tiny spark of awareness activates. Half a second. Just enough to ask: am I reaching because I am hungry, or because this is what I always do? That half-second changes everything. It is the difference between autopilot and choice.

These suggestions are embedding themselves deeply into your subconscious mind. They grow stronger every day. Stronger every evening. Stronger every time you sit on that couch and your hands stay still. They are firmly planted. And they belong to you.
[--- COUNT OUT + HOMEWORK ---]
Now I am going to count from zero up to five. With each number you become more alert, more awake, more refreshed.

Zero. Closing the door to the subconscious mind. Sealing in the 8 PM Circuit Breaker. Sealing in the Kitchen Closure. Sealing in the Hand Awareness. Sealing in the evening of choice. Everything we built today is locked in, growing stronger by the hour.
One. Slowly beginning to come up.
Two. More physically aware. More mentally alert. Knowing that tonight is different. Tonight the kitchen closes at 7:30 and the evening belongs to you.
Three. Coming up higher. Feeling lighter. Feeling clearer.
Four. Eyes beginning to open.
Five. Eyes open, wide awake. Fully alert, refreshed, and ready for a new kind of evening. Welcome back.
One, two, three, four, five. Eyes open, wide awake.
[--- POST-SESSION HOMEWORK ---]
Here is your homework. Three things.
First. Tonight and every night this week, close the kitchen at 7:30. Physically. Wipe the counter. Close the cabinets. Turn off the light. Make it a ritual. The kitchen is closed.

Second. Log what happens at 8 PM. Just a few words each night. Did the craving show up? How strong, 1 to 10? What did you do instead? How long did the craving last before it passed? This log shows us the pattern breaking in real time.

Third. Before you sit on the couch each evening, choose one thing you will do besides eat. It does not have to be big. Sketch for ten minutes. Call someone. Do some gentle stretching. Just one thing that is not food. Choose it before you sit down.

If you have a night where the old pattern runs, do not punish yourself. The Circuit Breaker is installed. It may not catch every evening immediately. But it is there, and it gets stronger with every repetition. What matters is that on at least one night this week, you close that kitchen and discover that the evening is fine without food.
I will see you at Session 2.

cases.title: Weight & Medical: The Hormone-Driven Cycle
cases.presenting: My doctor says I need to lose 40 pounds or I am going on insulin. I have been diabetic for 5 years. I have sleep apnea. My body feels like it is working against me. I have tried everything. Surgery scares me. The weight loss drugs are not covered by insurance. I do not know what else to do.

client.name: David L.
client.history: Type 2 diabetes diagnosed 5 years ago, currently on metformin. Sleep apnea with CPAP prescribed but used inconsistently. BMI 38. Carries weight primarily in the abdomen. Physician has stated clearly: lose 40 pounds or insulin injections are next. Has explored gastric sleeve consultation but is scared of surgery. Applied for Ozempic but insurance denied coverage. Gym membership purchased 6 months ago, attended 3 times. Feels defeated and hopeless. Wife cooks healthy meals but David snacks at the office and takes seconds at dinner. Insulin resistance makes weight loss physiologically harder. Frustrated by the sense that his body is working against him. Resting heart rate 82. Blood pressure controlled with medication. No psychiatric history. No alcohol or substance issues.

intake_dialogue.text: David, tell me what brought you in today. In your own words.

My doctor gave me an ultimatum. Lose 40 pounds or go on insulin. I have been diabetic for 5 years and it is getting worse. I have sleep apnea too. I use the CPAP machine sometimes but honestly I hate it. I feel like my body is a machine that is breaking down and I cannot stop it.
That is a lot of medical pressure. Tell me about the weight loss attempts. What have you tried?

Everything. I looked into the gastric sleeve surgery but I am terrified of going under the knife. My doctor wanted me on Ozempic but the insurance denied it. I bought a gym membership and went three times. Three times in six months. My wife cooks healthy dinners but I snack all day at work and I always go back for seconds at dinner. I know what I should do. I just cannot do it.
When you say your body is working against you, what does that feel like? Physically.

I am tired all the time. The sleep apnea means I never feel rested even when I sleep eight hours. My knees ache from the weight. I get winded going up stairs. And the diabetes thing is cruel. My doctor explained it. The insulin resistance means my body stores fat more easily and burns it harder. So even when I try to lose weight, my body fights me. It is like trying to run uphill in mud.
Tell me about the snacking at work. What does that look like?

There is always food in the break room. Donuts, cookies, someone brings in bagels. And I have a drawer in my desk with trail mix and granola bars. I tell myself it is healthy snacking but I go through a bag of trail mix in two days. During tax season it is worse. The stress eating kicks in and I am eating nonstop from March to April.
And the seconds at dinner. Your wife cooks healthy food. What happens at the table?

She makes a reasonable portion. I eat it. It is good. And then I look at the pot on the stove and I think, just a little more. And the little more turns into a full second plate. She does not say anything anymore. She used to. Now she just looks at me. That look is worse than the words.
What about the CPAP? You said you use it inconsistently. Tell me about that.

I hate it. The mask is uncomfortable. I feel claustrophobic. I rip it off in my sleep half the time. My wife says I snore like a freight train without it. I know it is important. I know the sleep apnea makes everything worse. But putting that thing on my face every night feels like admitting I am broken.

Let me ask you something important. The insulin, the surgery, the medications. Those are medical interventions and they may be part of your path. What I do is not medicine. I cannot change your A1C or your insulin resistance or your sleep apnea. What I can change is the behavioral layer: what you eat at work, the seconds at dinner, whether you use the CPAP, whether you move your body. Those behaviors are driven by your subconscious. That is where we work.

I understand. I am not looking for a miracle. I just need something that helps me actually follow through on what I already know I should be doing. Because knowing is not the problem. Doing is the problem.

clinical_notes.theory_of_mind: Multiple biological headwinds complicate this case. Insulin resistance promotes fat storage and inhibits fat burning, creating a physiological barrier to weight loss. Metformin may affect appetite unpredictably. Sleep apnea disrupts the cortisol, ghrelin, and leptin axes: poor sleep elevates cortisol (promotes abdominal fat storage), increases ghrelin (hunger hormone), and suppresses leptin (satiety hormone). CPAP non-compliance compounds the sleep disruption. The 88 percent has encoded a learned helplessness belief: weight loss is impossible for me, my body fights me. This belief becomes self-fulfilling because it undermines behavioral follow-through. The conscious mind has all the knowledge but the subconscious has installed defeat as the default response to health challenges. The medical complexity means hypnotherapy is ONE tool in a multi-disciplinary approach, not the whole solution.
clinical_notes.ep_approach: 58% Physical lane approach: direct, literal, body-centered. Use your body responds, you feel the change, notice the physical sensation. Kinesthetic VAK: anchor suggestions to physical feelings, body weight, muscle engagement, the sensation of the CPAP mask, the feeling of fullness at dinner. Direct commands work: your hand stops reaching for the desk drawer, you put the fork down after one plate, you put the CPAP on and keep it on. For the Emotional component (42%): soften with some permissive language around the fear and defeat. Mix direct body commands with permission-based emotional processing.
clinical_notes.key_reframe: Your body is not working against you. It is responding to the signals it receives. Insulin resistance, elevated cortisol, disrupted sleep: these are signals in a feedback loop. We cannot change the medical signals with hypnosis. But we CAN change the behavioral signals: what you eat at work, how much you eat at dinner, whether you use the CPAP every night, and whether you move your body every day. The medical system handles the chemistry. We handle the choices that feed the chemistry.
clinical_notes.contraindications: TYPE 2 DIABETES: must coordinate with physician. Do NOT promise A1C improvement, medication reduction, or any medical outcome. Sleep apnea: must coordinate with sleep specialist. CPAP adherence is a medical compliance issue; hypnotherapy supports behavioral compliance but does not replace medical direction. If physician prescribes insulin, do NOT suggest hypnotherapy as an alternative. If gastric sleeve surgery is reconsidered, support the client through pre-surgical anxiety but do NOT advise for or against the procedure. This client requires an explicit SB 577 scope-of-practice conversation at Session 1 and a brief scope reminder at every subsequent session. Screen for depression: medical defeat and hopelessness can mask clinical depression. If depression is present, refer to licensed MHP for concurrent treatment.
clinical_notes.root_cause_assessment: No single childhood root cause. This is a multi-factorial adult-onset pattern. The diabetes diagnosis 5 years ago created a fear response that paradoxically increased eating (stress eating as coping). The sleep apnea creates chronic fatigue that reduces motivation for exercise and increases reliance on food for energy. The CPAP avoidance is driven by claustrophobia and a symbolic resistance: wearing the mask means accepting being broken. The work snacking is environmental and stress-driven (tax season amplification). The seconds at dinner are habit plus the insulin-resistance-driven delay in satiety signaling. The gym abandonment reflects all-or-nothing thinking: if I cannot do it perfectly, I will not do it at all. The learned helplessness belief (my body fights me) is the meta-pattern that ties all the behavioral failures together.
clinical_notes.neurochemistry: Insulin resistance: cells resist insulin, blood sugar stays elevated, pancreas produces more insulin, excess circulating insulin promotes fat storage, more fat increases insulin resistance. This is a medical cycle that creates a physiological headwind for weight loss. The behavioral layer we address: what food enters the system and when. Sleep apnea: disrupted sleep fragments cortisol rhythm, elevating daytime cortisol which promotes visceral fat storage and increases appetite. Ghrelin (hunger hormone) rises with poor sleep. Leptin (satiety hormone) falls. The result: the client is hungrier, less satisfied after eating, and stores more of what he eats as abdominal fat. CPAP compliance directly addresses this hormonal cascade. Metformin: may reduce appetite in some patients, may cause GI discomfort that is mistaken for hunger in others. The client should discuss any appetite changes with his physician. Stress eating at work: cortisol-driven, producing a dopamine spike from high-calorie foods. The office environment (visible food, social eating, desk drawer stash) creates constant cue exposure.
clinical_notes.evidence_base: Kirsch 1995 meta-analysis: hypnosis combined with CBT produced greater weight loss than CBT alone, with benefits increasing over time. Allison and Faith 1996: hypnotherapy subjects continued losing weight post-treatment. For medical comorbidity cases specifically: Bo et al. 2018 found mindful eating reduced binge episodes significantly even in metabolically compromised populations. CPAP adherence research (Weaver and Grunstein 2008): behavioral interventions improve CPAP use by 1.5 to 2 hours per night. Motivational interviewing and habit-based interventions outperform education-only approaches for CPAP compliance. Note: no published RCTs specifically test hypnotherapy for CPAP adherence; this application is based on behavioral modification principles applied to medical device compliance.

session_plan.pretalk_focus: Scope-of-practice conversation FIRST: what hypnotherapy can and cannot do for a diabetic client with sleep apnea. We address behaviors, not biology. The physician handles the medicine. We handle the choices. Theory of Mind applied to medical weight management: the 88 percent has encoded defeat. We update the subconscious belief from my body fights me to my body responds to the signals I give it. The signals we change: work food, dinner portions, CPAP use, daily movement.
session_plan.induction: Arm-raising (standard). Physical lane (58%): direct language, body-sensation anchors, power words. Your hand IS rising. You FEEL the difference. Your body RESPONDS. Kinesthetic emphasis: weight of the hand, pressure of the feet on the floor, physical sensations throughout.
deepeners: 5-0 Count with PHS (standard foundation, physical emphasis on body weight and heaviness)
Reactional x2-4 (deepen and test depth, physical lane responses)
Progressive Relaxation with medical body awareness (attention to the abdomen, the chest for breathing, the face for CPAP acceptance, the hands for work snacking control)
Control Room descent (industrial, literal: walking down into a control room where the body's systems are managed, dials and switches the client can adjust)
therapy: Medical Scope Conversation Installation: before any behavioral work, install a clear boundary in the subconscious. The physician handles the medical chemistry. Hypnotherapy handles the behavioral inputs. The client is not choosing between medicine and hypnosis. He is adding behavioral change to his medical treatment. If insulin is prescribed, he takes it. If surgery is recommended, he considers it. Hypnotherapy makes the behavioral changes that support and amplify the medical treatment.

Work Snacking Replacement Protocol: the desk drawer and break room are constant cue sources. Install a three-part protocol. First, the drawer gets cleaned out and restocked with portioned, low-glycemic options (the client's physician can recommend specific foods). Second, the break room trigger is intercepted: when the client sees food in the break room, a micro-pause activates. He asks: is this on my plan? If yes, take a portion. If no, walk past. The walk-past becomes easier each time. Third, stress eating during tax season is redirected: when work pressure builds, the first response is three deep breaths and a brief walk, not the desk drawer.

Seconds at Dinner: Satisfied Signal with Insulin Delay Awareness. Insulin resistance can delay the satiety signal. The client's body may need 20 to 25 minutes to register fullness. Install a dinner protocol: one plate, reasonable portion, eat slowly, put the fork down between bites, wait 15 minutes before considering seconds. After 15 minutes, check in with the stomach. The satisfied signal is there. It is just delayed. Wait for it. When it arrives, honor it. The pot on the stove is for tomorrow's lunch, not tonight's second plate.

CPAP Acceptance and Compliance Support: the CPAP avoidance is driven by claustrophobia and symbolic resistance. Address both. For claustrophobia: progressive desensitization in trance. Imagine putting the mask on. Feel it against the face. Instead of constriction, feel it as a seal. A protective seal. The air flowing in is clean, measured, perfect. The mask is not a cage. It is a breathing partner. For symbolic resistance: wearing the CPAP is not admitting you are broken. It is a strong man maintaining his machine. An accountant who manages the numbers. The CPAP manages the breathing numbers. It is a tool, not a verdict.

Exercise Identity Shift: the client bought a gym membership and went 3 times. The all-or-nothing pattern: if I cannot commit to the gym 5 days a week, why bother. Reframe: movement is not a gym membership. Movement is daily life. Park farther from the office door. Take the stairs for one flight. Walk for 10 minutes after dinner. These are not exercise. They are movement. And movement compounds. 10 minutes a day is 60 hours a year. The body does not need a gym. It needs to move. Start with 10 minutes. The subconscious builds from there.

Insulin Fear Processing: the threat of insulin injections is creating a fear response that paradoxically increases stress eating. Process the fear. Insulin is not failure. It is a medical tool. But losing 40 pounds may prevent or delay it. The fear is valid. Channel it. Fear that paralyzes is destructive. Fear that motivates is fuel. Convert the fear from a weight on the shoulders to a fire under the feet. Every healthy choice is a vote against insulin. Every walk, every portion controlled, every CPAP night is the body sending a signal to the pancreas: I am helping you.

Physician Coordination Offer: offer to communicate with the client's physician. A brief letter or call explaining the behavioral targets being addressed in hypnotherapy: work snacking reduction, dinner portion control, CPAP compliance, daily movement. This builds the multi-disciplinary framework and signals to the client that all his providers are working together.
session_plan.countout: Standard 0-5 with suggestion seal. Physical lane emphasis: sealing in the body-level changes. Zero seals every installation: the Work Snacking Protocol, the Dinner Satisfied Signal, the CPAP Acceptance, the Movement Identity, the Fear-to-Fuel conversion. All locked into the subconscious, all working with the medical treatment, not against it. Five brings full alertness with physical energy, a sense of the body as an ally, and clear resolve about tonight's dinner, tonight's CPAP, and tomorrow's movement.

Explicit SB 577 scope conversation: what we can and cannot do. Theory of Mind with medical context. Suggestibility testing. First induction. Install Work Snacking Replacement Protocol. Homework: clean out desk drawer, restock with physician-approved options, log all work eating for one week.

sessions.title: Dinner Portions and Satisfied Signal
sessions.focus: Review work snacking logs. Deepen trance. Install Dinner Satisfied Signal with insulin delay awareness. One plate protocol: eat slowly, fork down between bites, 15-minute wait before considering seconds. Process the wife's silent look: partner as ally, not judge. Homework: one plate at dinner every night, wait 15 minutes, log whether the satisfied signal arrived.

sessions.title: CPAP Acceptance and Sleep Quality
sessions.focus: Address CPAP avoidance directly. Progressive desensitization to the mask in trance. Reframe from broken to maintained. Install nightly CPAP routine as non-negotiable self-care. Connect better sleep to reduced hunger, reduced cortisol, reduced cravings. Homework: CPAP every night for one week, log hours of use and how you feel in the morning.

sessions.title: Movement Identity and Exercise Reframe
sessions.focus: Address the all-or-nothing exercise pattern. Install Movement Identity: 10 minutes of daily movement, not a gym membership. Stairs, parking, after-dinner walk. Process the gym failure without shame. Exercise is not punishment for being overweight. Movement is celebration of what the body can do. Homework: 10 minutes of intentional movement every day, log what you did.

sessions.title: Insulin Fear Processing and Motivation Alignment
sessions.focus: Process the insulin threat. Convert fear from paralysis to fuel. Address learned helplessness: my body fights me becomes my body responds to the signals I send. Reinforce all behavioral installations. Mid-journey SMART review. Homework: write down three things your body did well this week.

sessions.title: Stress Eating and Tax Season Inoculation
sessions.focus: Address the seasonal stress eating pattern (tax season). Install stress response redirect: pressure at work leads to three breaths and a brief walk, not the desk drawer. Rehearse high-stress scenarios in trance. Build resilience for the next high-pressure period. Homework: practice the stress redirect at least once per workday.

sessions.title: Self-Hypnosis and Medical Maintenance Integration
sessions.focus: Teach formal self-hypnosis for daily maintenance. Integrate all installations into a single 90-second morning practice: breathe, visualize the day's food choices, feel the CPAP acceptance, see the 10-minute walk. Stress inoculation under simulated medical pressure. Homework: daily self-hypnosis, continue all behavioral logs.

sessions.title: Graduation, Physician Update, and Long-Term Plan
sessions.focus: Final SMART baseline review. Celebrate behavioral progress without making medical claims. Offer to send a behavioral summary to the physician. Reinforce all installations in a final deep session. Install maintenance anchor: hand on the abdomen, feel the body working with you, reactivate all behavioral commitments. Discuss long-term: self-hypnosis schedule, when to return for booster sessions, what to do if insulin is prescribed. Graduation: the body is not the enemy. The behaviors feed the body. The body responds. The medical team handles the rest.
